subsubtopic: SENDING OF PUBLIC OFFICIALS TO FRANCE FOR LANGUAGE TRAINING-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, recently the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) was quoted as saying that Canadians, particularly in the Toronto area, have a cry-baby attitude with regard to the recession and recent budgets. What the hon. member and his colleagues fail to understand is that, if Canadians are crying, they are shedding tears of rage and frustration caused, for example, by such actions as sending the likes of Ed Clark of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to Paris on a year's sabbatical, and Ms. Janet Smith of the Privy Council Office to the south of France for four months to study French, both at the expense of the taxpayer, at a time when the government is cutting the incomes of old age pensioners. That the government start listening to what Canadians are really saying and cut wasteful and extravagant spending such as that mentioned in the examples above.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: HIRING OF TEMPORARY EMPLOYEES BY REVENUE CANADA- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Recently the Minister of Labour circulated employers across Canada urging them to eliminate overtime for their employees in order to share all the available work and so reduce unemployment. At the same time as the Minister of Labour was making this appeal, Revenue Canada was hiring temporary employees who were told that they would only be employed for 18 weeks even if they had to work overtime to finish their work. The only possible purpose for such a directive was to prevent these employees from qualifying for the unemployment insurance benefits they would be entitled to if they had worked for 20 weeks. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That the Minister of National Revenue be instructed to direct his department to rescind that very unfair decision which is so detrimental to the rights of the employees hired to process income tax returns.

UNITED STATES PROPOSAL TO LOWER EXPORT PRICES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. There is a threat of a grain price war if the United States government goes ahead with its export credit buy-down program that would subsidize commercial credit rates by up to four percentage points. This move would have, as its ultimate effect, the lowering of grain prices for all grain exporting countries. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That Canada communicate its concerns at once to the United States Department of Agriculture and that Canada, in conjunction with other grain exporting countries, impress upon the U.S. administration that a lowering of grain prices will not necessarily sell more grain but will only sell grain at lower prices, causing hardships for producers in all exporting countries.

subsubtopic: URBAN TRANSPORTATION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Forty-seven per cent of Canada's total petroleum consumption is in the transportation sector, and 20 per cent of Canada's total petroleum consumption occurs within urban boundaries. Reasonable and significant reduction in petroleum consumption can be achieved through proper urban public transit. The Urban Transportation Assistance Program terminates next year, and if discontinued will seriously affect the ability of provinces and municipalities to provide suitable mobility for their citizens, as well as failing to take advantage of the possible decreases in need for imported oil. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper):
That the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources ensure that the Urban Transportation Assistance Program be continued and strengthened to benefit Canadians who live in urban areas, to benefit the Canadian economy, and to benefit energy self-sufficiency.

subsubtopic: EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the loss of $2.3 billion in Canada's foreign exchange reserves last month, almost equivalent to our total reserves, demonstrates the total failure of the high interest rate policy of the government in defending the Canadian dollar. Since Canadians cannot afford to lose another $2.3 billion, and we certainly cannot afford the high interest rates which are killing many of our industries, has the Minister of Finance any new proposals for the House to head off the impending fiscal and monetary crisis?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, of course the hon. member again has used false terms in describing this situation when he talked about the loss of currency. That, of course, is an error; it is wrong, a mistake, misleading, and totally false. I have pointed out more than once that when U.S. dollars are spent from our reserves, Canadian dollars are acquired. These dollars become part of our cash balances and are used to finance the requirements of the government. To call them a loss is an error that the hon. member ought to get out of his head.

subsubtopic: EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR
speechtext: I suppose the minister is going to tell us that the $2.3 billion spent to support the Canadian dollar was not spent, that it stayed there all on its own, and that the high interest rates which have been kept much higher than they should have been by the minister's policies were not high at all-they were just low, low, low, in comparison to the United States. He knows interest rates in this country are two or three percentage points higher as a result of his policies.

Madam Speaker, since there is some speculation in the markets today to the effect that the government is going to call in the IMF to bail it out, would the minister state whether or not any approaches have been made to the IMF and whether or not this is an option the minister is holding as an ace in the hole?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Absolutely not, Madam Speaker. That allegation is as inaccurate as the hon. member's first question. There is absolutely no intention and there has been absolutely no contemplation of any such action. We have substantial holdings of foreign exchange at the present time in the amount of almost $3 billion. We have access to $7.5 billion U.S. in the form of standby credits. In addition to that we have gold
reserves in our foreign exchange holdings with a market value of almost $7 billion U.S. So why go to the IMF, I wonder.
Because it would be the ultimate cop-out on the part of this government, because it does not have policies to deal with the situation.

RAILWAY FREIGHT RATES-APPLICATION OF GOVERNMENT GUIDELINE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. In the minister's budget speech last Monday night he said that price increases for services provided under federal jurisdiction would be restricted to the 6 per cent and 5 per cent two-year guideline. Since transportation was specifically mentioned, can the minister tell the House whether railway freight rates will be restrained to that 6 per cent and 5 per cent level, since there is a clear perception in the minds of the public that that is what the minister intended?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: RAILWAY FREIGHT RATES-APPLICATION OF GOVERNMENT GUIDELINE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what 1 intended to say was that the government expected the regulatory agencies, in establishing rates in the various fields mentioned, including transportation and communications, would observe the 6 per cent and 5 per cent rule unless justification existed for a contrary course of action. That is the policy, and it will be implemented in various ways by the government.

subtopic: ROLE OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
ROLE OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure the minister knows that the CTC does not regulate freight rates. They are merely filed and published. Is the minister intending to bring in legislation to effect the 6 per cent and 5 per cent guideline?
July 6, 1982

Furthermore, since public communication was specifically mentioned, can the minister tell the House whether he intends to instruct the CRTC to limit the latest CN-CP Telecommunications application, which is calling for increases at the level of 25 per cent to 30 per cent? Is the minister going to ask the CRTC to restrict those increases to the 6 per cent and 5 per cent guideline level?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: ROLE OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we have already indicated to the regulatory agencies, including the CRTC, that we wanted the 6 per cent and 5 per cent guidelines to be observed. As I mentioned yesterday, in the normal course these boards will examine applications and make their findings. If in their conclusions they exceed the 6 per cent or the 5 per cent rate, then it will be up to the government to determine whether any such abridgement of the rules is justified. If it is not justified, it will be overturned where the law permits the government to do so.

subtopic: ROLE OF CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we would be very interested to know how this will be implemented inasmuch as many of the regulatory agencies do not have that residual power in legislative form to dictate what the rates will be.

Madam Speaker, I would like to address another supplementary question to the Minister of Finance. Inasmuch as the minister is calling upon the provinces to invoke similar action with services which are provided under provincial jurisdiction, what sort of response did the minister receive from the provinces in the recent meeting held last week as a result of his budget? Are the provinces going to comply with the minister's suggestion that the 6 per cent and 5 per cent guideline should be followed in those services which are provided under provincial and/or federal jurisdiction?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I regret that I cannot throw light on that question because I was not present at the meeting between the Prime Minister and the premiers of the provinces.

Madam Speaker, 1 want to follow up on the questions which the minister has been dealing with concerning the important matter of prices. Could the minister tell us whether the cabinet has sent quite specific guidelines to all the federal regulatory agencies to ensure that prices will be kept, in terms of increases, within the 6 per cent limit? More specifically, can the people of Canada rest assured that Bell Canada's rates will not go up more than 6 per cent; that CN's and CP's train tickets and Air Canada's plane tickets will not go up more than 6 per cent, and that that institution endeared by every Canadian, the Bank of Canada,
Oral Questions
will be forced to hold its increases within the prescribed rates laid down by the government?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED ABSENCE OF ADEQUATE MEASURES TO CURB PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I also have some questions for the Minister of Finance, since the answers he gave just now were far from clear. If I remember correctly-perhaps the minister will agree that I am right, unlike my colleague whom the minister accused of being wrong three times just now-the November budget was based on the principles of equity and justice. How can the minister invoke these principles today, when he is putting a ceiling of 6 per cent on wage increases for federal employees and is unable to give us the assurance that the same ceiling will apply to price increases, particularly those made by fedeeral agencies? In the circumstances, could the minister inform the House whether he still believes in or supports the principles of equity and justice with respect to people who are being penalized because of a lack of sufficient measures to control price increases?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLEGED ABSENCE OF ADEQUATE MEASURES TO CURB PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, I take it for granted that the hon. member also subscribes to the principles of equity and justice. I do. Yesterday his leader stated that the proposals which we made with respect to wage restraints, in his view, were a step in the right direction. 1 wonder if the hon. member shares the view of his leader on that point. I did not hear his leader suggest that we bring in an over-all system of price controls, which seemed to the implication in the hon. member's question.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE JUSTIF1ABLE SALARY INCREASES INTO ACCOUNT
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE JUSTIF1ABLE SALARY INCREASES INTO ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary.
This is not the first time the minister has failed to answer a question. He knows perfectly well that Canadians are very worried about the possibility of price increases. Yesterday the minister, in referring to federal agencies and Crown corporations, said that in cases where there was sufficient justification, the matter would go before the regulatory body, which would determine whether or not there would be an increase. If inflation does not go down to 6 per cent next year, could the minister inform the House whether he is willing to justify, before the regulatory body, wage increases that are now subject to restraint and have been reduced by the budget? Is the minister prepared to reconsider wage increases on the same terms as a price increase that would seem to be justified?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE JUSTIF1ABLE SALARY INCREASES INTO ACCOUNT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is our conviction that if we get the co-operation of all the partners in the economy it will be possible to bring down price increases to 6 per cent. That is a possibility that can be achieved if we do receive the co-operation that is required. Then, of course, the impact of all these changes that have been mentioned, including the wage restraint, will be minimized as we get ourselves into a 6 per cent world of recovery, rather than remain as we are now in a 12 per cent world of stagnation and recession.

subsubtopic: NATIVE FOOD FISHERY PROSECUTIONS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It concerns the western fishery. The House resumed, from Monday, July 5, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government, and the amendment of Mr. Wilson (p. 18905).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in introducing his budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said:
The government has pointed the way to recovery, but it alone cannot get Canada on the move. We must tackle this task together.
Canada is one of the most fortunate nations in the world. We have tremendous natural resources. We have well-educated and competent workers, and we are better equipped than many countries to survive the worldwide recession. However, we want to do more than merely survive. We want to work our way out of the present difficulties in a way which leaves us well positioned to take full advantage of the upturn in the world economy when it comes.
The budget measures in themselves are worthy of serious attention, but before addressing them I would like to echo the minister's call for all Canadians to involve themselves in serious consideration of how best we can shoulder our responsibility to work our way out of current difficulties and prepare for better times.
Budget bashing is a traditional Canadian occupation. It is traditional that special interest groups respond with more and more requests to help their particular situation; it is traditional that opposition parties attack and give no credit for positive measures. In our present situation, budget bashing can easily become Canada bashing. Financial markets are skittish and respond in an exaggerated way to any evidence of political division or uncertainty.
But Canadians have a remarkable ability for compromise, for working together to overcome difficulties, for balancing the
need of regions, of minorities, of conflicting groups so as to arrive at the common good. This is a time that calls for all our goodwill and all our patriotism and pride in Canada.
Two years ago, on May 21, 1980, this House was united in a way we rarely see. Statesmanlike speeches on the Quebec referendum results were made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), and it may be useful today to remind ourselves of that spirit and of some of the statements made then.
The Leader of the Official Opposition described the referendum vote as "an expression of pride and belief in this country in which we can all joyfully share" and spoke of uniting Canadians in "a common determination to build a renewed federation which can make this a stronger country, a richer country, and a better country in years ahead".
The Leader of the New Democratic Party said:
We have ... reached a level of political maturity of which all civilized nations of the world are envious. . . . last night we showed that we can get along together despite deep differences.
Later in his speech, he said:
Fishermen in Newfoundland, farmers in Saskatchewan, miners in Sept-iles and people in every region of Canada must see the federal government as an ally, as their government. This is our objective.
The spirit which animated this House on May 21, 1980 is needed again as we face difficult times to which we can find solutions by working together.
At this time of very delicate balance, it is important that we all play a constructive role-otherwise, to quote the Financial Post, "The extreme and the implacable, egged on by the excitable in the media and unable to see merit in a middle way, may blindly help precipitate" a crisis for Canada.
Canadians are concerned about inflation, about high unemployment, about the deficit, about high interest rates; consumer, business and investor confidence are at a low ebb. To deal with all these problems requires a careful balance and mix of policies.
Most people who talk to me are more concerned about unemployment than about inflation. As long as people are working, they usually can manage in one way or another to deal with increases in the cost of living, but being unemployed takes the heart out of people. Yet we know that if inflation goes unchecked we will lose our competitive position in world markets and the long-term result will, in fact, be more unemployment. Therefore, inflation must be addressed as a high priority.
In inflationary times people try to protect themselves by negotiating higher wages, but when wages and prices chase each other, purchasing power does not increase; a 12 per cent increase does not improve the situation of a family if prices have also gone up 12 per cent.
July 6, 1982

One measure that the government proposes in the budget is to limit increases for Members of Parliament, civil servants and staff of Crown corporation to 6 per cent next year and 5 per cent the following year. It is hoped that provincial governments and the private sector will follow this example. To be sure, public servants have not caused inflation and have no responsibility for it any more than other Canadian citizens. Those who were expecting increases higher than 6 per cent next year will naturally be disappointed, but this country has been built on sharing and on working for the common good, and if limiting an increase to 6 per cent helps to create jobs for Canadians who are unemployed, helps to protect our future, I think most people will agree to that limit.
Federal regulatory agencies are being asked to restrain prices of the goods and services that they control. The provinces are being asked to do the same in their jurisdictions as part of a two-year national effort to reduce inflation.
Unemployment is at a higher rate than most of us have seen in our lifetime; the expectation that Canadians may find and hold a job and plan their future on that basis is threatened. It is important that we move quickly to deal with unemployment, not only because of the distress to the individual and family but also in terms of the economy as a whole. Unemployed people do not pay taxes as they did when they were employed; businesses which are in difficulties do not pay taxes and contribute to the economy as they do when they are prospering; and in fact, much of the increase in our deficit now is a direct result of the recession. The deficit is not growing because of increased federal spending; expenditures have been held in check, but revenues are down and unemployment payments have greatly increased.
Therefore, the government has to take prudent, selective measures to support the economy and preserve jobs and so, ultimately, help to contain the deficit. The November budget allocated some resources to job creation and the budget before us targets further resources for that purpose.
However, while direct job creation relieves immediate distress, helps people to maintain skills and perhaps acquire new skills, and can have other values in terms of improving communities, for long-term job creation we must look to a dynamic, confident private sector, and particularly to small business which has traditionally played an important role in job creation.
High interest rates, depressed sales, production cost increases and other factors have presented our private sector with difficulties that have challenged all its resources and ingenuity.
To help business cope with the present and prepare for the improvement in world markets which must come, the budget includes a set of tax proposals that lower the tax on interest income and on capital gains on selected investments. The measures proposed will result in significantly lower interest rates in priority areas-the housing sector and borrowings for new investment by small businesses, farmers and fishermen.
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
The proposals also increase the attractiveness of equity investment for individual Canadians. These proposals have received less attention than they deserve in the discussions on the budget so far. Perhaps they are not regarded as being firm since a committee has been established to examine them. Indeed, some have said that these measures should be put in place immediately. However, since they are quite innovative and involve new financial instruments, surely it is wise to test them with experienced accountants, lawyers, economists and business people before they are actually put in place later this year.
Canadians can feel just pride in our private sector whose enterprise has made possible a standard of living and social security system which is the envy of many countries. Success in revitalizing the private sector will also protect Canada's advanced medicare, unemployment insurance, pension, education and other programs essential to social justice and social progress. Over the past 20 years Canadians put in place a social security system which avoids the excesses or shortfalls of some countries while reaching out in support for all Canadians.
In difficult times there is all the more reason for society to help those in need. That is why, although this budget will hold the increases in old age security to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in the next two years, those senior citizens in need who qualify for the guaranteed income supplement will continue to receive fully indexed increases and they can also receive a supplement in order to offset fully the limitation on indexation of their old age security payment.
Similarly, while family allowances will for the next two years increase by 6 per cent and 5 per cent rather than by the full cost of living, in order to ensure that this limitation does not hurt families with modest incomes the child tax credit will continue to be fully indexed and increased by $50 for the 1982 taxation year.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that difficult times always bring with them requests for radical reappraisal of all our economic programs and policies. This is a healthy and constructive exercise. The more one understands of constraints, international and domestic, the better the chances of being able to advance practical solutions. This budget represents a sane middle-of-the-road approach which tries to reduce inflation, increase confidence, create jobs and hold the line on the deficit while protecting social programs.
If all Canadians can work towards those goals, we will survive the present recession, we will be prepared to take advantage of world recovery when it comes and make full use of our great advantages so that we continue to be one of the most prosperous, stable and progressive nations of the world.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech I just listened to reminded me of speeches I used to hear from Buckingham Palace on Christmas Day 25 years ago. Smooth sounding but with very little substance; reassuring, but nothing substantive to prove an argument. The hon. member, in defending the Liberal budget, said that if we remain calm-I am paraphrasing her now-and all segments of the community

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
get together and restrain themselves, then inflation will come down and happy days will be here again. However, she neglected to say-and I hope this does not sound like a cheap shot because we are all in this bag together-that it is a lot easier for her, the Conservatives and myself with incomes around $60,000 to $65,000 gross a year to give that advice to our constituents than it is for them to follow.
So 1 just hope that the Liberal backbenchers realize that they cannot go home to their constituencies and tell the unemployed, those who are on mother's allowance and welfare, to hang in, tighten their belts, restrain themselves and happy days will return. That is not the way it is done. The Canadian constituency has grown very old and very wise in the last two years. They realize that most of their financial problems, in a personal way, are directly related to the non-thinking which has been going on in the Liberal cabinet since the last election.
Until June 28, Mr. Speaker, the majority of Canadians who were hurting at least had hope. They thought there was some light at the end of the tunnel. But as a result of the June 28 budget most of that hope is gone because most of the light at the end of the tunnel has disappeared.
I am very briefly going to touch on three or four major issues in the budget and then I want to pinpoint three major aspects which are either in or not in the budget.
1 think it is absolutely cruel that at a time of tight and expensive money, when consumer demand is down with the resulting massive lay-offs and unemployment of about 1.5 million, the government has decided to constrict consumer spending power even further by taking some $2.6 billion out of circulation, money which is badly needed to stimulate the economy in a recession which is bordering on an absolute depression. For example, tax increases of the order of $1.3 billion; the scapegoating of the public sector by saying that civil servants-and by implication all wage and salary earners-are the major cause of this inflation. That is nothing but patent nonsense and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and his cohorts opposite know it. Real wages, in terms of purchasing power, have declined by 10 per cent over the last six years. Now the government is saying that purchasing power is going to decline another 5 per cent or 6 per cent in the next year because it admits that inflation is going to remain at 9 per cent or 10 per cent.
Another very cruel aspect of this budget is the partial deindexing of family allowances and deindexing of pensions. I should add here that former government employees now retired paid an extra 1 per cent contribution to their pension plans as a hedge against inflation but now that has arbitrarily, and 1 think illegally, been withdrawn. And they have no clout and no way in which to fight back.
On the supply side, again we are slavishly following President Reagan. But maybe we should not blame President Reagan; we should go back to Mr. Bouey, Governor of the Bank of Canada, in 1975 when he started it all with this supply side economics. We are going to give tax breaks to business. Well, normally tax breaks do result in an increase in investment in business, but at a time when more than 30 per cent of our plants is underutilized, those tax incentives are going to
fall on barren ground. There is no possible way that those small tax incentives will fill that manufacturing and productivity gap of between 69.2 per cent and 100 per cent capacity. There again is another major blunder on the part of the Minister of Finance.
Now we come most certainly to the focal point of the budget and the focal point of our economic woes today. That, of course, is the interest rate in this country which is absolutely outrageous. It is the principal cause, almost the sole cause, of business bankruptcies, farm foreclosures, massive unemployment, a general malaise in the economy and an emotional depression that is spreading across our country. This budget as of June 29 has only exacerbated the problem of high interest rates, about which I will go into detail a little later.
Suffice it to say that high interest rates are strangling our economy and the finance minister has sluffed off the whole problem. He has put it into the hands of so-called experts who often cannot agree among themselves. They are to report back in three months' time, three lost months as businesses slide under, as farms go out of business and as unemployment increases. The Minister of Finance has again sluffed off the whole problem of interest rates for another three months, supposedly to be included in yet another budget next fall.
There are other inequities, such as controls in public sector salaries and later in private sector salaries, as I have mentioned. There is to be a reduction in pension increases, a reduction in family allowances and so on.
This budget lacked a new economic strategy. There is no new economic program in it. Senator Olson came forth with a paper in 1980 in which he outlined a prescription for recovery and prosperity. This was based on resource megaprojects. These projects are all down the tube. They were all highly capital intensive at a time when the cost of money was skyrocketing. They were low labour intensive. They did not create the jobs which the manufacturing sector normally would. The megaprojects are, at least for the time being and for the foreseeable future, finished.
This budget which the Minister of Finance had the nerve to introduce on June 28 makes no reference whatever to an alternative economic strategy to bring us out of our economic doldrums. There is nothing whatever. Again, the minister has used the band-aid, quick-fix approach so characteristic not only of the Minister of Finance but indeed of the government which has ceased to govern. That is why the New Democratic Party has called repeatedly since the budget was introduced for the Liberals to have the common decency to step down from power and hand it over to those who are not only willing to govern but have some intelligence about how to govern this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are three major parts of this budget to which I want to make reference in some detail.
July 6, 1982

First is the premise on which the budget is based. Repeatedly in the House of Commons during question period the Minister of Finance has said: "Look, fellows, we do not have a high interest rate policy, we have an anti-inflation policy. If we bring down inflation, interest rates will come down, businesses will get turned around, unemployment will drop as the demand for goods and services increases." I say balderdash to that because the Minister of Finance also likes to make reference to things which happen south of the border. The Liberals are great ones to blame others. From the day the Prime Minister was elected, I do not think he has ever admitted he was wrong about anything.
Let us take a look at what is happening in the United States. Inflation in that country on an annual basis has now declined to 6.5 per cent. But where are the interest rates? The prime interest rate in the United States of America is still over 17 per cent. Where is unemployment now that inflation is down in the U.S.? Unemployment in the United States is just under 10 per cent. Yet the Minister of Finance has premised the logic of his budget on the United States model. The U.S. model is not working. Interest rates are remaining high, businesses are remaining strapped financially, and unemployment is high, widespread and causing considerable anguish in that nation. So much for the minister's model and so much for his reference to fighting inflation which in turn will automatically, according to him, bring down interest rates and unemployment, all of which is nonsense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think he believes in fairies too.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Second, there is no new economic strategy in the budget. There is nothing to replace the failed resource-based projects which, as I said earlier, were highly capital intensive when money was very expensive. There was no hint of a move to an industrial strategy to end the branch plant approach.
I would like to expand on the branch plant approach right now. I was very gratified last Wednesday evening when our Conservative friends supported us in our subamendment to the budget calling for a stronger FIRA. That was a complete turnaround on the part of the Conservatives. I am overjoyed that members such as the hon. members for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) and Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) joined with socialists in this corner and said "Enough is enough: we cannot afford to have our industrial sector bought out any more by loosening up FIRA." We were united on this side of the House to strengthen FIRA. It is the Liberals who now want to loosen FIRA.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Tories would vote for anything to dump the Liberals.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Somebody has just said the Tories would vote for anything to dump the Liberals. That shows how much creative thinking they put forward in the House these days.
On page 7 of the budget we find the following:
First, the threshold for review under the small business procedures will be raised from $2 million and 100 employees to $5 million and 200 employees for new investment or direct acquisitions in Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
Second, where a foreign-controlled Canadian company is acquired in the course of the acquisition of its parent or another foreign-controlled company, the small business procedures threshold will be $15 million and 600 employees.
FIRA has been greatly abused, but there is one thing FIRA has done. It has reduced the acceleration of a U.S. takeover of our industrial sector here in Canada. The reason we in the New Democratic Party are opposed to loosening FIRA's regulations is because the branch plant economy is not good for Canada.
In the 1950s and 1960s it is true the branch plant economy gave us an accelerated rise in our standard of living. It produced jobs, it built warehouses and distribution centres, and in a limited sense it was beneficial. A recent study has strongly indicated that since 1976 the branch plants in this country have created a net outflow of $1.5 billion in capital. So it has not been beneficial as far as capital intensity and capital investment in this country are concerned.
Second, branch plants are very soft indeed on research and development. Most research and development is done by parent companies back home, and "back home" is usually Indiana, Ohio, Iowa, Chicago or wherever.
Third, when times get tough it is branch plants which shut down first or lay off First or pull in their financial horns and say: "We have to close." There is no way that branch plants will compete with their parent companies back in the United States.
With respect to the Foreign Investment Review Agency, we have heard many Conservatives, some Liberals and many businessmen in the country say that the Americans do not like FIRA and therefore it is shutting out capital investment in Canada. This is more of a perception than a fact or reality. Since FIRA was implemented, 91 per cent of all applications have been accepted. I think it is atrocious, it is sad and it is deplorable; I do not know why we hear all the whining on the Conservative benches, all the whining by their business colleagues and their corporate friends outside the House. It just does not make any sense.
Let us look at the other side of the coin or, more appropriately, the other side of the border. I should like to refer to an article which appeared on page 9 of The Financial Post of March 13 entitled: "U.S. stringent on foreign investment." It was written by Nicholas Patterson and reads in part:
First a look at some of the federal restrictions.
He was referring to United States federal restrictions with respect to foreign investment in that country. He continued:
The report says: "There are a number of U.S. restrictions which prohibit direct investment by non-resident aliens in enterprises engaged in intercoastal shipping, domestic radio, television, telegraph, domestic air transport, mining on federal land, hydroelectric power and atomic energy."
This means that in the U.S. it's illegal for a Canadian company to control a telephone company. In Canada, a U.S. company. General Telephone & Electronic Corp., controls British Columbia Telephone Co. Does that sound like investment reciprocity? In the U.S., the policy is that a foreigner, including a Canadian, can't get an offshore oil or gas exploration licence. In Canada,

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
offshore exploration is dominated by U.S. companies. The same goes for uranium mining. Where is the reciprocity in that?
The article continued and was very enlightening. I hope Conservatives and business people across the country realize that the Americans have even tighter restrictions on foreign investment in their country than FIRA ever had.
The Americans have a Buy America Act which was brought in at the time of the great depression by Franklin Roosevelt. It means that a very large percentage-and I believe it is 50 per cent at the federal level and at the state and municipal levels very often it is higher-of all government procurement of goods, products or whatever it happens to be must be from American companies. We still do not have such a provision in Canada.
We have listened to the Conservatives, who have gone full circle historically. They used to be the protectionists, traditionally and historically. The Conservatives now want to sell out every square foot of factory space in the country for a quick buck to help us out of a time of economic distress. But we in this party are saying we should tighten FIRA laws, otherwise when the recession is over in the next two or three years, if it is over, we will end up with 65 per cent or 68 per cent of our manufacturing sector owned by foreigners, not 57 per cent, as at present. Let us not be foolish at this time of economic restraint.
There are two ways of approaching our major problems as we in the New Democratic Party see them. First, there must be a long-term structural change in the economy, a transfer of emphasis from resource-based megaprojects, most of which are based upon non-renewable resources, to a reindustrialization of the country which is job or labour-intensive and produces jobs at the rate of about $100,000 per job rather than the several millions of dollars per job that it costs in resource industries.
Second, in the short term we are talking about injecting capital into the economy at a time when there is plant underutilization to the tune of 31 per cent and at a time when there is an extreme downturn. On the one hand we are calling for a restructuring of our economic goals or a redirection away from the resource-based megaprojects to the employmentintensive industrial sector. On the other hand, in the short term we are saying, "Let us pump money into the economy now to get it moving again." This is not inflationary. It will not overheat the economy because, as I said a moment ago, we are underutilizing our plants.
The traditional Liberal policy is to gain short-term prosperity by selling off our resources to pay for our imports. That is the historical Liberal approach. But the megaprojects have fallen victim to the recession and the government must recognize the manufacturing sector as the engine of economic growth and recovery. Last year there was a $21 billion deficit in trade and manufactured goods alone. This helped to pressure the dollar down, and the government also failed to create the 200,000 jobs represented by that deficit. In the United States 24 per cent of the work force is in manufacturing; in Canada it is only 19 per cent. Again this is caused by reliance
on imported manufactured goods and selling off unprocessed or semi-processed resources to other countries.
Imports also drive down the value of the dollar. Incidentally, at the present time the government is bragging about its positive balance of trade. The reason for the net favourable balance of trade in this quarter and in the previous quarter is that Canadians cannot afford to buy imports. We are not importing the way we were during more prosperous times. This is not because of any great genius sitting on the treasury benches; it is not because of the Minister of Finance or any deliberate plan.
The plight of the country today is that we cannot afford the imports we would normally purchase. In the long run this may be a good thing. If the dollar dropped to 70 cents, we might then have to use our own initiative and creative capacity. We might have to start thinking about a change and we might return some backbone to government which is responsible to the people of Canada. Indeed, we might begin to manufacture goods which over the years we have allowed to slip away because it was easier and for a while cheaper to import them from offshore. I think those days are over.
Also the fact that we have to import so much in the way of manufactured goods drives up interest rates, which is another major cause of the depression that I mentioned at the outset. We would target certain industries where we have the largest deficits, such as the machinery industry. In 1981 Canada had an appalling deficit of $6.9 billion in its trade of machinery, or a loss of 69,000 jobs just in machinery industries alone. I represent the federal riding of Brant where there are two major farm implement manufacturers, Massey-Ferguson and White Farm. The government has made great efforts to try to keep these two companies afloat. I appreciate it personally and on behalf of my constituents. There was an ILAP designation for Brant. There were loan guarantees to Massey-Ferguson and several millions of dollars to White Farm for research and development. There will probably be in excess of $50 million of capital infused into the local economy as a result of ILAP.
The long-term prospects for my constituency are good, but let me look at the two agricultural industries. Last year, 1981, in the agricultural equipment field alone we had a net deficit of $1.3 billion, which represents a loss of 13,000 jobs in Canada despite a trade agreement with the United States. 1 notice that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is listening to my remarks at this point. He would be interested to know that when Massey-Ferguson and White Farm were going full steam ahead a few years ago, their combined workforce in Brantford was approximately 5,000. As well, there were approximately another 2,000 workers in Toronto, which made a total of 7,000 workers.
If we did not have this net deficit in trade and agricultural equipment vis-a-vis the United States, we would be employing twice the number of agricultural implement workers than we are just in the City of Brantford, and this was during the good times. Today, Massey-Ferguson is down to about 1,400
July 6, 1982

workers from a workforce of 3,000 or 3,200. I understand this morning that White Farm is down to approximately 400 from a workforce of 1,200. This is one area where much can be done to return jobs to Canada without being protectionists or economic nationalists. We simply say that during tough times you must look after yourself first and then, if you have enough left, go abroad.
The story of the mining and construction equipment sector is a sad one, too. Finland mines about one-third of what we mine in Canada but our mining companies buy two-thirds of all their heavy underground mining equipment from Finland and Sweden. What a loss and embarrassment that is. What the hell has this government been doing for the last ten years? Not much. It has been plastering one band-aid on to another and pretty soon the whole bag will fall through. In fact, it already has.
There is a $563 million deficit in power generation equipment. There is a $898 million deficit in industrial machines. There is a deficit of $1 billion in machine tools. Last year these deficits were higher than Canada total balance of payments deficit and this is all in the manufacturing sector.
We would target the transportation equipment industry. We would establish Enterprise Canada, a Crown Corporation capitalized initially at $2 billion, to promote research and development in those healthy industries. We would promote those forward-looking, third wave industries in high technology in order to hold on to them, because I very much fear that if the Foreign Investment Review Agency is tampered with as a result of this budget, we will lose those small but up-front, state of the art, third wave high technology industries in Canada, as suggested by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) during question period yesterday. Those businesses are small and vulnerable, and as sure as I am standing here, "Silicone Valley North" will rapidly become "Silicone Valley South", controlled or owned outright by the Americans.
Finally, we would then force agreements on the multinationals if we could not make amicable agreements to make sure that for every dollar of sales that the multinationals enjoy in Canada, we must have a dollar's worth of production here. What is wrong with that?
I see that you are rising, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that my time is up. I could go on but I will not seek the indulgence of the House for extra time. I simply want to say what the classical Greeks said, that those whom the Gods hate, they first make mad. The gods obviously must hate this government.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with dismay to the attacks which have been made against the budget in the past week. I have read Hansard as well as the newspapers. I personally believe that this budget outlines a positive course of action toward economic recovery. This is true whether I look at it from the viewpoint of my constituents in Essex-Windsor, from the viewpoint of the
The Budget-Mr. Whelan
food and agriculture industry or from the viewpoint of the nation as a whole.
My constituency is one that generally represents the content of Canada on a percentage basis. It is approximately 95 per cent urban and 5 per cent rural. I believe that I have a good understanding of what is happening in our country.
As my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) pointed out last week, the task before us is to bring down inflation and increase productivity in order to get our economy going again. I will reiterate some of the proposal the Government of Canada has made to lead the country toward this very desirable goal. I realize that some of these proposals have already been mentioned but I do not think it hurts to repeat them again.
Some of the proposals involve cutbacks in pay increases to cabinet ministers, MPs and senators; ceilings on pay increases for more than one-half million federal employees; limits on indexation of personal tax exemptions, family allowances and old age security benefits; restraint in price increases regulated by federal agencies; $750 million in spending for job creation and economic development incentives as well as $300 million to help Canadians buy homes. There is an extension of programs to stimulate home renovation.
With respect to co-operative housing, I was very much involved with co-operative housing in a co-op organization I was associated with before I came to this place. It had rough times and tough sledding then. I remember when we allowed people in co-op housing to establish their rent as a downpayment over one year and rent was about $60 a month at that time. Therefore, you know how long ago it was, Mr. Speaker. I was in the Toronto metropolitan area when we were involved in those operations at that time.
Another proposal provides for the construction of new rental units and to offset problems with mortgage renewals. As well, there is $400 million to reduce interest costs for small business undertaking new investment. There is $200 million to be made available through the Farm Credit Corporation for farmers to refinance debts at lower interest rates. Consultations are to take place with the private sector on proposals that could be implemented this fall to reduce taxes on Canadian investment and to reduce interest rates for small business, farmers, Fishermen and buyers of new homes.
This is a comprehensive and positive package. A number of these measures are of particular interest and benefit to the agri-food industry and I would like to explain them in a bit more detail.
First, the special farm financial assistance program. The government recognizes the severe economic difficulties facing many farmers in certain sectors of our agricultural community. In the past year interest costs have grown to become the leading input cost in Canadian agriculture, accounting for almost 20 per cent of total production costs. Last November we set aside $50 million to help farmers desperately in need to refinance their total debt load. Under this program, 382 farmers were given much needed interest rate reductions. Now

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Whelan
that assistance will be offered to a further 1,600 to 1,800 farmers over the next few years.
This should be measured against bankruptcies. It is said that the maximum you must save from bankruptcy is 261 farmers who needed assistance last year, who did not receive it and went bankrupt. Some of them, no matter how beneficial a program could have been worked out, could not have been assisted anyway because they were that far down the road. Some of the economic plight or conditions they found themselves in took place before high interest rates, as shown if one checks their financial statements. As I said, this measure could help at least 1,800 farmers.
That does not mean that we will not continue with the right of the Farm Credit Corporation to enter the private money sector even in a bigger fashion than it has been involved before. Loans will be made at the going FCC interest rates for this special program to which I have just referred. Now the going rate is 16.5 per cent, but with an interest rate rebate of four percentage points for the First two years of the loan, and loan limits for the individual farmer, he or she will be able to borrow $300,000. Jointly, a farm partnership will be able to borrow $500,000. That is the maximum which will apply under those conditions.
The funding for this program comes from the budget allocation of $100 million and a reallocation of $116 million from existing Farm Credit Corporation funds. That is not all. Farmers will be able to continue to borrow money from other places.
Second, there is the small business investment grant. Both incorporated and unincorporated Canadian businesses, including farmers, are eligible to share in this $400 million federal interest subsidy program. Interest rate reductions under this program of up to four percentage points will be available for loans for new assets, such as farm buildings, machinery and equipment. The program covers loans of $10,000 to $500,000 for purchases made between June 28 this year and March 31, 1983.
One of the very important aspects of this program which has received little publicity so far is the fact that expenditures for scientific research are also eligible for interest rate reductions. I would certainly hope that the agribusiness and food industry firms take advantage of this provision to boost their research efforts in the next few months. The grocery products manufacturers of Canada spend less than one tenth of one percentage point on research. 1 hope they are listening. I hope they study this legislation. Maybe we can get them up to 1 per cent. Anyhow, they spend very little, so little that one can hardly measure it. They spend the least amount of any group in Canada. I hope they grab on to this incentive and go ahead with it because research in food production is our most important tool.
The small business bond, as set out in the November budget, will remain in place until the end of the year to help farmers and other small businesses refinance debt at reduced interest charges. The federal government is offering tax concessions to
commercial lenders which should enable these lenders to make refinancing loans at just a little over half the normal lending rate. We know from experience that these programs can be worked out and be very beneficial for many people in the farming community and in the small business operations of this country.
The new budget also contains a new capital gains reserve provision that answers many of the concerns expressed by farmers following the November budget. Anyone studying the ways and means motion will see what I mean. This provision is more liberal than the one proposed last December 18 and was modified from the November 12 budget. So, I think what is being offered at the present time is pretty darned good and that most in the farm community will be well satisfied with it.
I know that the agricultural community also has a special interest in the proposal to change the tax system to permit significantly reduced interest rates, perhaps three to six percentage points below the prevailing rates, on loans for new capital investment in this country. At the time we were debating the recent amendments to the Farm Credit Act in this House, many members of this House, many members on the agriculture committee and many farm groups indicated their support for special tax concessions to investors in farm mortgages. I am sure this support will again be voiced during the consultations which will take place, as outlined by the Minister of Finance last Monday night.
Wherever possible, the federal government will hold price increases in regulated sectors to 6 per cent in the coming year and 5 per cent in the following year. This could affect industrial milk producers and egg and poultry farmers, but not in the way in which many people think it will. Many think that those who are in regulated agencies or marketing boards will suffer tremendously. Let me tell Your Honour that the people in marketing boards are inflation fighters. They have accepted a form of control that no one else in our society will accept. Through Your Honour, 1 intend to outline to the House why and how this is taking place.
So many people in our society condemn marketing boards but they do not know anything about them. The only thing they know about them is what someone else said about them. They have never studied them. 1 recently addressed over 300 people at a meeting in British Columbia. Before the meeting I asked them for their opinions on marketing boards. Nearly everyone condemned them. When I then spoke to them in a forum, I asked: "How many of you have ever studied a marketing board?" Only two out of the whole group had so studied. The remainder were basing their opinions on editorials or radio commentaries. I would say that 99 per cent of the people who make those comments or write those articles have never ever studied marketing boards and what they do.
Let me just go into a few details as to how these price ceilings will be applied. For instance, concerning the regulated agencies, they are still being worked out, but 1 would offer a few observations on this point. Prices in the regulated sector which we are discussing have been below the general inflation
July 6, 1982

rate in the past year. Therefore, if everything else were in the same category, we would probably be asking people to accept these rates.
I will state some figures. Retail prices for dairy products in May were 10.9 per cent more than a year ago, but that is below the national rate of inflation. Poultry products were only 1.48 per cent more expensive than in May, 1981, and eggs were actually 2.66 per cent cheaper than a year ago. Therefore, how will a regulated agency be affected? Some farm leaders said: "What a terrible thing this will be!" Some of them should check what is going on in the regulated industries because, for instance, whole milk production in Ontario only increased 5 per cent for the whole of last year, and that is below what we are asking them to accept for the first year. We are asking that for the second year. Therefore, if the input costs are down, if everyone is productive and these people will meet some of the production figures, we will be inflation beaters and be very productive at the same time.
Producer prices for eggs have dropped four cents a dozen in the past 12 months. I am referring to producer prices, not retail prices. Producer prices for chicken and turkey have dropped three to five cents per kilogram. Producer prices for industrial milk have increased by $4.01 per hectolitre, or 11 per cent in the last year. That is also below the national rate. Because of the current weakness of feed grain prices, we do not expect the formula prices for eggs and poultry to trigger increases of more than 6 per cent in the coming year.
As I said, many people in our society, even in some farm organizations and some who are going bankrupt, are actually the biggest condemners of marketing boards. Many consumers think that marketing boards lead to higher and higher food prices, but that is just not so. Canadian marketing boards have a good track record as inflation fighters. I do not mind repeating that over and over again. That is because it is contrary to what some of our so-called brilliant economists in the country say. I know that Your Honour is very familiar with brilliant economists. I believe you obtained your economics degree from the University of Wisconsin. For instance, the Ontario vegetable marketing board has many members, some of them from the constituency of the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) who is present in the House, and some from my own constituency of Essex-Windsor. They have negotiated prices for processing vegetables this year which, on the average, are only about 5 per cent higher than they were in 1981. These farmers are doing that because they recognize some of the problems in our nation. Provincial marketing boards are doing this. How many headlines or commentaries have hon. members seen about what they decided to do this year?
At the same time, Ontario producers are increasing productivity, mainly because an incentive was provided by the federal government and by the Ontario government. For instance, we have placed a tariff on tomato paste to give tomato growers protection of 13.4 per cent, plus a devalued dollar. The province came in and gave outright grants of several million dollars to build tomato paste facilities. That means there will be thousands of acres of tomatoes, hundreds of thousands of
The Budget-Mr. Whelan
dollars will be spent, more jobs will be created in southwestern Ontario, and it will cost less than anyone ever estimated, not a 9 per cent, 10 per cent, 12 per cent or 14 per cent increase but, rather, a 5 per cent increase.
Take the price of pumpkins. Some people get $30.75 per tonne. If any of you ever buy a pumpkin, you will find you will pay $2 or $3 for it. Weigh it and then see how much the farmer receives for that pumpkin. He receives only 3.4 per cent more than last year, that is all.
Carrot prices are $72.30 per tonne. That is 4.8 per cent more than in 1981. The highest increase was for green and wax beans, up 7.5 per cent at $226 per tonne. These are products that are for canning, for processing.
Overall food price increases for 1982 are expected to be less than 10 per cent, and this easing in food price inflation is certainly good news for Canadian consumers. Individuals can keep their own food budgets from rising by even this amount by substituting seasonal Canadian fruits and vegetables and frozen and canned produce for costly imports of fresh produce. For instance, many Canadians think they have to have their head lettuce from Florida, Arizona or California. They might as well just take a good drink of water. There is no food value in head lettuce whatsoever. It has a little cellulose in it. If you want to eat something that is good and nourishing, many people say: "Who are you to tell us what to eat?" Well, we make a study in our department of what people should eat. The scientific evidence is there that cabbage will do you much more good and has many more proteins, vitamins and minerals than the costly head lettuce that you bring into Canada from the deep south about seven months a year. You can store it, you can keep it under controlled temperature storage. The temperature-stored cabbage will last for one year and it will be all Canadian. I see the member from Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) opposite. He knows that in Agassiz and in Saanich-ton on Vancouver Island they are growing cauliflower all year round, except for six weeks in the year. If that industry expands, as we think it will, a big part of western Canada can be supplied by cauliflower all year round. It is excellent cauliflower; I have eaten it. They have shipped it here and I have eaten it there. Right in the stores in British Columbia there is Canadian cauliflower for two-thirds the price of American cauliflower, but because people are not used to eating Canadian cauliflower, they do not think it is as good. We know it is better, because those things that grow in the northern climate grow more slowly and it takes more time to take the nutrients out of the soil. Those products are better for you than those products that grow down south very fast. They have more of the things that you and I need to make a healthy living. How do you think I have grown so strong and feel as young as I do as the Minister of Agriculture? And I have been in politics in Canada for 20 years! It is because you are what you eat.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Right on!

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Whelan

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If I last as long as the former member for Prince Albert, that means that perhaps for 26 more years you will have to put up with me!
I am just saying that we have the potential for production here in Canada. Canadian farmers and food processors know first-hand the problems that inflation has caused in our industry. I know that they support the government's effort to bring down the inflation. General Foods, which is one of the largest produces in North America, has sent us a telegram saying: "We are prepared to do that kind of thing; we are prepared to co-operate with the government." That is the kind of thing that you like to hear.
I am sure the hon. member knows full well the potential for productivity in this product. The member for Fraser Valley West and those for some of the other parts of Canada, such as Saint Jean in Quebec and similar areas, know the potential for producing this Canadian food for our own consumption and for export.
The Minister of Finance has called on the provinces, on private industry and on all Canadians to share in the fight on inflation. Canadian farmers, as I said, have already been in the front lines in this fight. Some can say that they are bearing the cost of inflation. They are still surviving, though.
I see here an hon. member from Saskatchewan. Fast year in that poor province of Saskatchewan land values went up 25 per cent! That government in Saskatchewan did such a good job of making people so rich they all turned Conservative!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They left them with a big deficit, but I see that they are not going to get rid of the finance corporation; they have to have that Crown corporation so they will have more money to lower gasoline prices.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would just point out to the hon. minister that there was not a big deficit left in Saskatchewan. I would prefer that the minister would keep his speech correct.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There was not a big deficit? He knows that I know that they left it in such good financial condition that that is why they turned Tory. Those across the way have not made one suggestion to help the Government of Canada. As good Canadians they should be making some constructive suggestions about what we should be doing. They have not made one that I have heard, and I have checked the record very thoroughly, too.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Stick to the truth. Put it in high gear. You have a big lead.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are talking about the provinces and what they should be doing. I am told that the provinces are ready to do this. Premier Buchanan of Nova Scotia has already taken a step in the right direction. That is not a rich province; it is a province which has great financial difficulty. But that Premier has recognized the need across the country, to make sure that Canada stays alive.
When we talk about fighting inflation, we find that in the front lines there are the farmers there, and there are many others willing to join them in the front lines. Cost increases have outstripped price increases in many commodity sectors. Farmers not practising supply management have had little protection against the ravages of inflation. They have not had the 10 per cent, 12 per cent or 15 per cent wage increases that public servants, Members of Parliament and private industry employees have had in the past year. And yet, if other sectors of the economy had the same kinds of increases in productivity as the agricultural industry has had, we would have a much stronger economy today. So what is the member talking about? To listen to the member from Brant (Mr. Blackburn), you would think that no one in Canada was increasing productivity.
Just the morning after the budget was brought down, Mr. Speaker, my colleague the minister responsible for Statistics Canada and I announced the findings of the 1981 census of agriculture. We talk about efficiency. You hear some economists and other people talk about inefficiency because they are in a marketing board. Milk production rose by 7 per cent in the last five years, not went down, as some of the figures given by a previous speaker would suggest. Yet Canadian farmers produced that milk with 12 per cent fewer cows! Is that what you call inefficiency? There were 1.77 million dairy cows in 1981 compared with 1.99 million dairy cows in 1976.
In the poultry sector the number of laying hens declined by 12 per cent in the past decade, but the number of eggs rose by 10.5 per cent from an annual average of 209 eggs per bird to 241. Efficiency in agriculture is increasing all the time, Mr. Speaker.
Many words have been spoken and written about the budget in the past eight days. This House has heard a mixture of praise and criticism, statistics and economic theory, political rhetoric and personal opinion. In light of these varied observations, it is easy to be blinded and to fail to see the forest for the trees.
Some of the members opposite are concentrating their vision on the size of the deficit; the deficit should be lowered by massive cuts in government spending, they say. Others are looking at the number of housing starts; there should be a tax cut on construction materials, they say. More? Where? How? Where are the trade-offs these critics would make? Is it easy? It is easy for the opposition to say they would not have a $19.6 billion deficit, but they did not tell the public what increases in taxes and cuts in programs they would have to make to accomplish this. This past Sunday in my constituency in a little village called Comber, a rural community, the Tilbury West council under Reeve Jack Morris decided to give leadership to go ahead and build a senior citizens' complex, self-contained apartments. I do not know why the press did not report it, but at the meeting I said that it had cost $600,000 for these 27 units and that the majority-97 per cent-of the interest rate is subsidized by the federal government; so that the total
July 6, 1982

interest rate a tenant would pay on a subsidized unit was 2 per cent. I knew many Conservatives in the audience. Many Liberals were there. There were probably a few New Democrats, but they did not say they were. However, I asked whether they wanted us to cut that out. Did they want us to stop that expenditure? We were building those homes for senior citizens who had made such a great contribution to our nation. Did they want us to stop that 14.5 per cent or 15 per cent interest subsidy we were giving on these units? I asked them, please, to tell us if they wanted us to stop those government expenditures we are so bad at making.
Do hon. members opposite want me to cut expenditures for the Farm Credit corporation or for beef stabilization? What cuts would they make in Agriculture Canada's program? Many times in recent months hon. members opposite have criticized me for not spending enough on agriculture. The budget for which I am responsible has decreased from 2.4 per cent of the federal budget to about 1.5 per cent of the federal budget, but has agricultural efficiency decreased? No. Agricultural production has increased. The incomes of farmers who have looked after themselves have not suffered very much. Some have said I should have a $1 billion budget for the Farm Credit Corporation, and I have said I would like to have that. It has been said that I should spend hundreds of millions of dollars to help beef producers.
My department is making very good economic use of taxpayers' money. We are improving our services to the agricultural industry every year, yet our share of the federal budget is declining. We are able to do this by being efficient and by having a good economic ship with a good crew. We have an excellent crew in the Department of Agriculture, which is the most decentralized department and knows probably better than any-better than many; that is for sure-what is going on in this country. That is the way it has been since confederation. Agriculture Canada has been spread across the country. There are over 10,520 employees. About 2,500 of them are here in the capital area, and the rest are all over Canada. The people in my department understand what is going on in Canada and report to us what is going on. As I said, we are able to do this by being efficient, and I do not believe hon. members or the public could find much to cut out of my already very lean budget.
It is all very well for another political party to say it would not put a ceiling on civil service wage increases and that it would create more jobs, but it does not tell the public how. What alternatives are hon. members opposite offering? I remember when the right hon. member from High River was Prime Minister. High River is where he was born; I forget the name of his riding.

speechtext: Yellowhead.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Toronto Star of October 20, 1979 said: "Clark backs more interest rate hikes". The other day the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said, I believe on a
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan
hotline program in Montreal, that he has no alternatives. That is what was reported to me. When he was Prime Minister he backed the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I never heard that he sued the Toronto Star or reporting what he said incorrectly.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are ready to rise. I want to refer to one other matter, and I will be as brief as I can.
Who is Pierre Bourgault? He was a leading separatist in Quebec. What did he say, as recorded in the Montreal Gazette? He wrote an article in his own hand. It was copied in the Ottawa Citizen. It was not copied in the Windsor Star. Why? The Windsor Star did not copy it because it was too positive for a separatist to say. This is what he said:
Let's count our blessings.
Did I say blessings? Yes I did, because by comparison, we are blessed beyond reason.
I add "in Canada".
A transportation strike? A doctors' strike? Irrelevant. Interest rates? Unemployment? Inflation? The Quebec budget? Insignificant. The fall of the dollar? The economic crisis? Trudeau, Levesque, Drapeau? Mere incidents.
Who are we to complain?
And yet we complain. And not without reason. We're not used to so many problems hitting us at the same time. We're used to being spoiled. We're used to our big and small privileges. And if we're deprived of some of them, we tend to imagine that we're deprived of our most basic needs.
I'm half-joking. Of course we're in a mess. But, at the same time, we musn't cry too loudly, because the rest of the world has every reason to be envious of our problems.
The kids on the Falkland Islands (British and Argentine alike) would rather suffer a Metro strike. I'm quite sure of that.
The population of El Salvador would rather go without doctors for a few days-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
