subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 must say I enjoyed the performance of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) here today. He is usually an entertaining speaker. In the farm halls of the nation and across the fields of the nation he can make quite a contribution.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And in the barnyards.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not exactly sure what the minister eats on a day to day basis, but I certainly know what he spreads

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan
around in this House. We are supposed to be talking about the budget, not the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, but the minister used most of his speech to discuss the estimates of his department. The estimates of the Department of Agriculture are not before the House.
When it comes to agriculture, I think hon. members on this side of the House would tend to agree with the minister, knowing full well that he has not been able to get the necessary funding for many agricultural programs. I certainly do not want to see any cuts in agricultural programs. The industry is basically a very productive and progressive segment of our economy, but we are not supposed to be talking only about one segment of our economy.
When the minister gets out of the hallowed halls of Ottawa and gets away from the insulation of Ottawa and goes about the country-I admit he does that a little more than many other ministers-and when the country is as perplexed, troubled and sick as it is today, I do not think people would appreciate a speech of buffoonery and faint sarcasm like the speech of the minister here today.
Every segment of our society is sick, but we in this House, whether in the opposition or on the government side, would not underestimate the bounty of Canada. What makes us feel so badly is that in spite of our bounty we have had a government for 14 years under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-except for a brief interval of six months-which has put our economy into dire straits, to coin the Prime Minister's own words.
I do not intend to belabour the Department of Agriculture estimates reviewed by the minister. There is little in the budget for the farm community except, to use the minister's own words, a reallocation.
I listened to the minister, and I wish he would stop grumbling and belching now. As I said, I do not know what he eats, but it certainly produces a lot of gas. I would just as soon he spread what he is spreading here across the fields of the nation. Farm productivity would certainly be enhanced.
The fact is that the little help in the budget for the farm community is mainly a reallocation of existing funds. In order to qualify for the small amount of assistance in the budget, a farmer would have to be in dire straits. If what the minister was talking about today is so good, why was it not in the November 12 budget or even in the first budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen)? No matter how sincere the Minister of Agriculture is-and I give him credit for being sincere in the interests of the farm community-the fact is that in the cabinet of which he is a member he does not have enough clout to get the funds necessary for agriculture.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the problem?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have a point of order. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is trying to tell the House I have done nothing. In his own riding we built a research centre at a cost of some $20
million. And the hon. member is not even on the government side of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister is not making a point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister knows well-and he is now making his exit-the history of that research centre. It took about 11 years from the time it was first conceived in the Department of Agriculture to the time it was finally built. It was on stream in 1957, 1958 and 1962 when a former member from that riding who happened to be of the same political stripe as I am had it finalized. It was the change of government in 1962-63 that deprived the farm community of Atlantic Canada of the much needed research station at Kentville, Nova Scotia. It became entangled in the political cross-currents in the land and it was only after two other research stations were built, due to the concerted efforts of the people, that the station was finally built. And I am proud it was, Mr. Speaker.
But enough of this distraction and diversion. The agricultural budget is not the subject of this debate. Today we are talking about the budget-the third confessional of the Minister of Finance of Monday, June 28. It may be appropriate that this is the ball season because I liken the Minister of Finance to that eminent batter of old called Casey, who swung three times. When he swung and missed the third time there was gloom in Mudville. What we heard from the minister on Monday, June 28 was certainly a message that cast gloom right across the country. It did not live up to the expectation that the minister stimulated when he announced the budget in a hurried fashion in the House not so long ago. Because of those expectations of a budget that was supposed to address some of the fundamental problems of the country, the dollar, the stock market and the buoyancy of the Canadian economy are all much worse today than before the budget.
If we need an example of the reason for this crisis of confidence, it was illustrated in the answer that the Minister of Finance gave to a question put by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) in question period today, who referred to yesterday's headline to the effect that Ottawa borrow $2.3 billion to prop up the dollar. The minister gave the most amazing answer and tried to suggest that this was an unusual thing and that it was not a loss when you had to borrow $2.3 billion to prop up a dollar that was sagging. If he could have given a full answer I suppose he might have tried to turn the loss incurred by the interest payment on that $2.3 billion into a profit by his figuring. Most of us cannot begin to appreciate sums of such magnitude and this is part of the problem.
The minister reminds me of the character in Alice in Wonderland. Alice was talking to Humpty-Dumpty who told her that when he used a word it meant just what he chose it to mean and nothing more or less. Alice said that the question
July 6, 1982

was whether he could make a word mean so many different things but Humpty-Dumpty replied that the question was which was to be master, that was all.
A headline in the business section of the Montreal Gazette today refers to the $2.3 billion that is needed to prop up the dollar. We must also consider the run there has been on the dollar since January and the money we have had to borrow to prop it up. Since January the government has taken action in the financial markets to defend the dollar by selling off $1.5 billion in foreign reserves, by borrowing almost $1 billion in standby credits from Canadian banks; by arranging standby borrowing from foreign banks of $1.5 billion; and by arranging for a new bond issue of $500 million, a total of $4,347 billion U.S. since January in order to try to keep our dollar at an artificial level.
Notwithstanding that massive injection of billions of dollars which cost our taxpayers a lot of money, our dollar has fallen three cents in that period. Of the $2.9 billion that there were in foreign reserves at the end of June, $2.4 billion or 82 per cent is represented by funds borrowed from abroad.
We are in dire straits with regard to our foreign reserves and that affects interest rates. This question was not addressed in the budget the other night. The Minister of Agriculture, who has left the House, can talk about stop-gap programs, but 1 agree with him that it is interest rates that is killing the economy, not this hocus-pocus of band-aid and postage stamp solutions.
1 want to come back to the matter of foreign reserves and put in simple terms what that $4.3 billion represents.
In his first budget the minister struck at the oil companies and at the energy program. In the next budget on November 12 he struck at foreign investment. I suggest that in this budget, as my leader suggested earlier in this debate, he struck at the people of Canada. By removing the indexing, in effect he is imposing a $1.3 billion tax increase.
As has been repeated ad infinitum in the House, senior citizens will find that their old age pension is capped. Anyone who suggests that a senior citizen whose income is just above the GIS qualifying level does not need help, does not understand the plight of our senior citizens. Not only will the old age security payment be partially indexed, but pensioners will be paying more tax due to the deindexing of income tax. Old age pensioners not eligible to receive the guaranteed income supplement, that is single people with total incomes above $8,500 and married couples with total incomes of about $14,300, will receive $80 less per person or $160 less per couple in 1983-84 because of the 6 per cent cap on indexing in 1983 and the 5 per cent cap in 1984. They may also have to pay more income tax because of the partial deindexation of the tax system. Meanwhile, upper-income taxpayers earning more than $30,000 per year continue to enjoy the full benefits of the reduction in marginal tax rates in the budget of November 12, 1981.
I suggest that the coach of this team that has the Minister of Finance throwing the pitches had better start finding a substitute for the world series in the fall. This capping of old age pension payments will come home to haunt the Minister of
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan
Finance and every member of the government as they go around their constituencies, if and when we ever have a summer adjournment.
It is not just senior citizens who are affected, of course, but those who receive family allowances with a 6 per cent cap. Anyone bringing up a family is faced with escalating food prices. The Minister of Agriculture may talk about some kind of program to maintain the price of food and may extol the virtues of marketing boards, but I should like to know how he will try to control the cost of the imported commodities that go into our food.
The question of unemployment was really not touched upon in the budget. We all know that very soon unemployment insurance premiums are to be revised. A story in The Globe and Mail of July 2 dealt with the sad state of the unemployment insurance fund. Last month payments from the fund showed a 41 per cent increase over the same period last year. More than $2.75 billion was paid out. I will read the whole story because it was tucked in to the back pages of the financial section of a lot of Canadian newspapers which were still trying to digest the budget. The Canadian Press story, which has not been refuted, reads:
The federal Government paid out more than $2.75 billion to unemployed people from January to April this year, a 41 per cent increase over the same period last year. Statistics Canada said yesterday.
Preliminary figures show that for the week ended April 17, claimants qualifying for benefits totalled 1.16 million, a record number.
The count was also 3 per cent more than for the previous month-when a drop is usually recorded-and 45 per cent more than for April, 1981.
That follows release of federal budget figures on Monday that forecast a $2.2 billion deficit for the unemployment insurance fund for 1982 instead of the $218 million shortfall predicted last November.
I will come to the deficit, Mr. Speaker. In fact, there is so much to say about this budget that time really becomes of the essence. The article goes on:
Employment Minister Lloyd Axworthy also confirmed on Tuesday that unemployment insurance premiums will have to be increased because of the soaring jobless rate which now stands at 1.25 million or 10.2 per cent. Mr. Axworthy said the Government would not announce the new premiums until the fall when more complete figures become available.
But Finance Department officials say premiums could rise to $2.50 next year for each $100 of insurable earnings, up from $1.65 this year. Rates for employers, currently $2.31, could rise to $3 or more, the officials said.
That is certainly an increase far above the 6 per cent that the minister is trying to get us to swallow. Then we have the really staggering punchline, because I was in this House when the unemployment bill went through and we warned about some of these problems. It says:
Earlier this year, StatsCan reported that Ottawa paid a record $4.8 billion in unemployment insurance benefits in 1981, a 10 per cent jump over 1980. The fund registered a $360 million surplus last year.
Payments this April amounted to $691 million, down 12 per cent from March but up 51 per cent from the $458 million disbursed in April, 1981.
The previous prediction of a $218 million deficit was based on Finance Department forecasts last November estimating average unemployment in 1982 would be 7.8 per cent.

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan
There are estimates that up to three million people could be unemployed at some time during the year.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that the minister predicted just seven months ago a deficit of $10.2 billion and then came into the House on June 28 and admitted-and goodness knows what it is going to be at the end of the fiscal year-that it is going to be close to $20 billion. Then we have a prediction for the unemployment insurance fund, which is a special account and not part of the total deficit, of a $218 million deficit; but in fact it is going to be more than $2.5 billion. Anyone in private industry or carrying on business by himself who was so out of kilter in his projections would have gracefully resigned, let alone be fired, for making such irresponsible projections.
I want to come to the point of just what is a billion and how you can relate to the billions the minister talks about in the deficit and the UIC fund. I went back and did a little research on Canada's budgets. There was a minister of the Crown who used to say "What's a million?" That was the Hon. C. D. Howe when he was being chastised for being so loose with public money. Now, of course, it is easier to say "What's a billion?", since we are into that realm. The billions just boggle the mind.
When I first came here as a member in 1965 the total budget was $6.5 billion. With supplementary estimates it got up to $7 billion. When the present Prime Minister took over, the total budget-not the deficit-was $10.2 billion. They were horrendous figures then, yet now we are talking about a deficit of some $20 billion. That is equivalent to someone overspending by almost 30 per cent. No wonder we are in difficulty; interest charges on the debt will be $45 million a day, which is equal to 9,000 taxpayers paying $5,000 in taxes every day.
This budget deficit is more than the total of all federal budgets for the first 74 years of this country's existence. We did not go over $16 billion in total budgets until the 75th year, the war year of 1942, when it went over $18 billion in total. That is the type of monstrosity we are talking about in terms of deficits and debt that this country is carrying. In effect, the debt represents 22 per cent of the budget, or $700 per person, $1,800 per taxpayer. When you stop to think that the average taxpayer pays approximately $4,000 in federal and provincial taxes, then almost 45 per cent of those taxes goes to service the debt. Is it any wonder that we have real problems in this country today when spending has gotten so out of control? We did not have a budget in excess of $2 billion until the fourth year of World War II, 1943, when we had a $4.3 billion budget. And all this money spent to service the debt does not provide one pension, make one medical payment, or help postsecondary education. It is, in effect, money out the window.
1 know my time is running out, Mr. Speaker, but one has to stop and look at the fact that it takes 75 years to exceed the $18 billion figure in total budgets, and then in one seven-month miscalculation the Minister of Finance comes into this House to report a $20 billion deficit and then has the nerve to stay on as Minister of Finance. That just shows the enormity
of the problem, one that is not going to go away with a waving of the wand like Merlin the Magician.
If things were not so serious, one might call this Minister of Finance the court jester of the finance ministers of the world. He likes to pretend that he is King Canute and can hold back the waves. For years, especially the last two or three, we have heard every possible answer to the problem of interest rates. Up until June 28 the minister has said there is nothing he can do about interest rates in this country. The problem is caused by other countries or the ugly Americans to the south. That was his answer month after month and year after year to the dilemma of high interest rates, certainly since the Liberals took power after the last election. The minister always said it was factors offshore that affected interest rates. Now out of the blue, realizing the deficit has risen to $20 billion in seven months from a $10 billion prediction-a 100 per cent miscalculation-let alone the run on the dollar of $2.75 billion, and the over $4 billion since January, those two factors most likely forced the minister to come into this House with a budget. Then he tried to bamboozle the people. But the people will not be bamboozled when the minister's answers for two years have been that interest rates were always a result of offshore events.
When we look around we see that interest rates in the United States are still 16.5 per cent. In Germany interest rates are 13 per cent and Japan is the only one with an interest rate of 6 per cent. France's interest rate is 14 per cent, as is Great Britain's. Switzerland's interest rate is 9 per cent and Italy's rate is 22 per cent. Canada's interest rate is anywhere from 17 per cent to 18 per cent to 19 per cent, depending on how preferred a customer you are. Some people pay over 20 per cent on their bank borrowings. Yet the minister brought in this 6 and 5 per cent tangle, about which he is supposed to excite Canadians and perhaps have them believe in him when Canadians have no reason to believe in him in view of the fact that he has struck out on two previous occasions. I suggest the way the stock market has reacted and the way the dollar has reacted since the Monday night budget means that the minister has also struck out again.
The only way this crisis of confidence in Canada can be resolved is to have a cleansing of this government. If this government is so proud of everything it has done, then it should go to the people with an election. The motion we are voting on tonight is that the government resign. Certainly if the Minister of Finance had any political integrity at all after he has led the Canadian people for two years down this deadend street of high interest rates which are crippling the economy, he would resign.
You can talk about all the billions of dollars worth of programs you want, Mr. Speaker, but there is one item which really focuses attention on the mentality which affects this place in terms of spending other people's money, that is, spending taxpayers' money. The other day my colleague, the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm), gave an example
July 6, 1982

of this. It is almost impossible for the public to appreciate what billions of dollars are. Even we cannot appreciate billions of dollars. But when you get some human story involving dollars misspent perhaps the figure can be multiplied and someone can understand what is meant when you talk about billions of dollars. The hon. member for Peterborough moved a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on June 29, 1982. It was not approved, of course. He discussed the case of one Janet Smith, an economic adviser in the Privy Council Office. An article was written about Janet Smith in the Peterborough Examiner on June 28, 1982. This was the same day as the budget. The article is entitled "Stop Janet Smith". It reads:
Public criticism of government's excessive spending has been less effective than it should have been. The reason in our view is that it lacked focus.
No more.
Last week the Privy Council Office announced that it will send Janet Smith to the Riviera to learn French. She will be there for four months. The bill to the Canadian taxpayer will be $11,800, plus her full salary.
Now, Ms. Smith is an economic adviser to the Privy Council. She is paid a salary of $75,000 a year. She is not, however, bilingual, as the job requires. Not for want of trying. She has tried and failed, a number of times.
The government felt that sending Smith to the federal language school in Quebec City would not work. She would be aware there of the issues of the day, and that would detract from her ability to learn.
Four months in the South of France, at public expense, was the obvious alternative. No issues, no money worries to distract her at Nice or Cannes or St. Tropez or whatever.
We make this suggestion with no tongue in cheek:
Every Canadian capable of writing a letter in either official language, or telephoning a government office or a Member of Parliament, should do so and issue the order clearly understandable in either English or French: STOP.
We should make it our business to see to it that Janet Smith, no matter what her difficulties with French, no matter what contribution she has made as an economic adviser to the present economic mess, does not get four months holiday in France at public expense.
We should make it our business to stop these gross abuses of public money.
I will not read any more, Mr. Speaker, because I see you have indicated that my time is up. But it is an interesting, ironic twist that on the very day of the budget this story breaks of an economic adviser in the Privy Council Office, well paid by any standard, going at taxpayers' expense, in the amount of almost $12,000, to France to try and develop a facility in French, for which we all commend her, when we have language schools in Canada that certainly should be able to do the job. That is absolutely symptomatic of the waste of taxpayers' money.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The situation will not be changed until we are able to change this government. The sooner we have that opportunity, the better it will be for the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at times such as these when we have several areas of international tension, pressures from international economic difficulties and dislocations in the marketplace, high unemployment which has become the mark of industrialized countries, and high interest rates accompanied by high inflation, governments must have underlying, long-term goals to overcome these enemies of man and management. While we talk
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
about long-term goals, governments must also be flexible in their policies to make sure that they arrive at those goals to recovery. If a policy does not work, then it should be changed and adjusted and no finance minister or any government should be hidebound or glued to interim policies that are not contributing to the long-term goals of recovery for the economy and smoother times for people in all walks of life. The major aims of the June 28 budget are to lower inflation and interest rates. In my view, interest rates are one of the biggest curses of all times. The budget is designed to help Canadians who are most in need of lower interest rates and the complimentary reduction in the Canadian rate of inflation. People buying new homes, whether they be existing ones or new ones, will get outright grants. Parents will receive a bigger child credit cheque. Business people will get significant relief from the high cost of money at the bank. Government tax revenues will be reallocated this year and next to activities that create jobs now and encourage new investment now. The thrust of this budget is to restore confidence, confidence in a future where inflation is reduced, and a future where new investment creates the jobs we need. If that confidence is not restored, you will not have money going into the economy and into development.
The size of the deficit is not due to massive government expenditures as some would have everyone believe. It is due to a lessening of revenues at the bottom and inflationary costs at the top. Therefore, unless inflation can be decreased the deficit will continue to increase at the top, and unless interest rates decline, the deficit will continue to grow at the bottom because there will be fewer taxpayers to provide for revenue.
It is important, then, that the June 28 budget set out to achieve the following: an attack on high interest rates; an attack on inflation; reallocation of funds to create jobs; a new housing package and new tax proposals. As a result, buyers of new homes will get a $3,000 grant on their purchases which will lessen interest charges. I am sure that other member's offices, like my own, have had many calls about this $3,000 grant. The forms will not be ready for ten days to two weeks but people will apply for the grants in the normal way through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Small business people will be able to get money at an interest rate 4 per cent less than the going rate for investment in plant and equipment. Farmers and fishermen, too, will be able to get money at this lower interest rate.
Long-term planning by any government is not complete unless we take into account some of the obvious issues or problems that lie ahead. We cannot always look at tomorrow morning. Whether or not we recognize it, we are in the middle of another industrial revolution. We are rapidly moving along in the change-over from manpower to the fast-moving era of high technology. Computerization is simply a household term. We are rearing children today who may have to be retrained two or three times during their lives. Education systems across Canada must be upgraded to meet the requirements of the

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
times, or they will be guilty of contributing to future unemployment, an unsettled work force and more costly production because many will have to continue to be trained on the job.
What about security? There will be very little security in many areas of employment unless we revamp and reform the diversity and the plethora of private pension plans across the country. Right now there are private pension plans in Canada from which a person cannot collect even in part until he or she has served the full required number of years. There are pension plans which do not pay the spouse a cent if the employee dies in the last year of service. The use of the survivor option must be put into practice even for surviving spouses to collect as little as 40 per cent. Some plans pay a flat rate benefit or so much for each year of service. There are other plans where an employee can work for 20 years, but if she or he is not 45 years of age, the person is deemed not to have a vested right in the plan and therefore, if laid off permanently, walks away from the job with nothing. This is true in plans where the employer contributes 100 per cent to the plan, but surely employees must feel that they have earned that money. Portable pension plans are a must if we are to look in a realistic way at the future which our children will face. Some provinces and the federal government have made minor moves in pension reform at their levels, but a major overhaul by the two senior levels of government is a necessity.
At the beginning of 1980 there were 14,600 private pension plans in Canada, covering 48 per cent of paid employed workers or 4.5 million employees. This coverage ratio remained virtually unchanged from 1978. The figures indicate that 54 per cent of males were covered by these plans and 38 per cent of females. For almost 60 per cent of private sector plan members pensions were based upon average earnings over the entire period of employment, even though it might be 35 or 40 years, or they were on a flat rate amount per year of service. By comparison, 95 per cent of public sector plans were based upon the higher earnings in the years just prior to retirement, for example the last six years. Two thirds of public sector plans had indexing provisions, while less than 5 per cent of private sector plans had automatic indexing which was generally limited to less than 3 per cent annually or a fixed dollar amount.
In 1979, $3.3 billion in private pension or superannuation benefits was paid to 829,000 beneficiaries, for an average of $3,930 per person. That is not a very big income, but $4,516 was the average for males and $2,929 was the average for females. An additional $8.2 billion was paid by old age security, guaranteed income supplement and the Canada and Quebec pension plans. Employee and employer contributions to all employer-sponsored pension plans amounted to $7.6 billion during 1979. Nearly two thirds of this amount was paid into trusteed pension plans with funds amounting to $52 billion at book value at the end of 1980. There is no danger of those pension plans going broke. This $52 billion in trusteed pension plans means cheap borrowing for governments and others who borrow from them. It is no secret that governments borrow from them. In Ontario the provincial government borrows
heavily from them. The CNR is known to borrow funds from its unions' pension plan. Other Crown corporations and provincial governments across Canada do it. As a result they are able to roll over their debt at very cheap rates of interest.
One does not need to be a great mathematician to realize that pension plans are wealthy and will continue to become wealthier if only a little more than $1 out of every $3 taken in on average is paid out in benefits. A Department of National Health and Welfare study entitled "Pension Plan Coverage by Level of Earnings and Age, 1978 and 1979" confirms that private pension plan coverage is low, although it increases with level of earnings. While 48 per cent of Canada and Quebec pension plan contributors are members of employer-sponsored pension plans, only 11 per cent of those people at the lowest income levels are covered by an employer-sponsored pension plan. However, 84 per cent of those with earnings in excess of $30,000 are protected by employer-sponsored pension plans.
Reform of pension plans across Canada will mean more money in circulation and less sitting in pension funds. In the long run it could also mean less demand on public funded pension plans and greater justice and fairness in pension plans themselves. Therefore it is incumbent upon us to move quickly in meeting the challenges of pension reform. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) listed four main goals of pension reform-all people should be able to belong to pension plans, private pensions must be portable, all pensioners should be protected from inflation, and women must be treated more equally.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has stated on many occasions that one top priority of government is to increase the guaranteed income supplement for single pensioners. She stated that this would be done as soon as resources permitted. This point now made, I must state that the most fundamental pension reform issue facing us is the continuing lack of adequate pension coverage. Without significant improvements in this area, other reforms will be meaningless for many Canadians. This kind of reform is in the true tradition of the Liberal Party of Canada, and we should act.
Some time ago a "W5" program on CTV gave a rather warped view of the activities of the Department of National Defence. It is important that the updating of defence equipment be placed clearly on the record. Because the Department of National Defence is very important in relation to any budget, I would like to turn my attention to a subject which is not often given the attention it merits. Of course, I refer to the Department of National Defence and the work of the Canadian military.
It must be greatly apparent to all hon. members that the current international environment is fraught with conflict- tensions in the Middle East, the Russian invasion of Afghanistan, tensions in Eastern Europe and in the Americas are rising, and there is renewed mutual suspicion in East-West relations. Although the SALT or START process, Strategic Arms
July 6, 1982

Reduction Talks, is continuing and the UNSSOD II is still in session at the United Nations, there remains an uneasiness in the western alliance. This uneasiness has been translated into a new awareness of the needs of national military requirements.
I am happy to note that the Canadian government acted responsibly in recognition of the changing strategic setting and has allocated substantially increased financial allotments to the Department of National Defence over the past two years. The minister told me that he is confident that when the strategic overview is presented to cabinet his department will continue to receive a substantially larger share of the federal budget than in previous years.
This year, the share of the federal budget to be devoted to defence expenditures is 9.6 per cent, which is not a bad share when considering there are approximately 32 government departments and many Crown corporations. This will allow the Department of National Defence to pursue its re-equipment program with vigour. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) is to be complimented for his efforts to re-equip the Canadian Armed Forces. It is obvious that he has some clout in cabinet and that is important to the members of our armed forces wherever they may be in the world.
The CF-18 Hornet fighter aircraft project is on schedule. The first of the 138 aircraft is due for delivery in October of this year. The final aircraft delivery is scheduled for late 1988 and the cost in today's dollars is expected to be about $5.2 billion.
The Canadian patrol frigate project is moving ahead. The two consortia involved in the design drawings for these are Saint John drydock in New Brunswick and Scan Marine in Longueuil, Quebec. All proposals will be presented to the department for approval and for a decision to award the contract. Some of the lessons learned by the British navy in the Falklands will be taken into consideration. New defence mechanisms to combat missile warfare will be included.
The next real milestone is in October of this fall, at which time proposals from the two contractors will be considered and the cost of these six frigates is expected to be approximately $2.6 billion in 1981 dollar value.
The Canadian Armed Forces and the militia units now have their full complement of general purpose armoured vehicles, such as the Grizzly, Cougar and the Husky. Those yet to come are for the logistics reserve. To date, 475 of the 491 vehicles contracted for have been delivered at a cost of $317.9 million.
As everyone knows, the Canadian Armed Forces have had an aging fleet of trucks to work with for some time. 1 am sure that no one was more pleased than defence personnel when they heard that a total of 2,767 of these vehicles have been ordered and the project is on schedule. The first one came off the assembly line on April 30 this year. The last one is to be delivered by mid-1985. The cost of this order will be $234 million in 1980 Canadian dollars.
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
All 128 Leopard tanks which were ordered some time ago have long since been delivered but a small quantity of support spares are to be delivered by December, 1983. Most of these tanks are now in Europe and the total cost was $261.5 million in 1980 dollar value.
All 18 long-range patrol aircraft, well known as the Aurora, have been delievered and are operating very successfully. Support spares are expected to be received until December, 1984 at which time the project will be completed. To date $450 million has been paid out for these out of a total cost of $582.6 million to 1984.
The present authorized military person-years for the Department of National Defence is 81,148 in the regular forces and 21,372 in the reserve forces. The authorized civilian person-years is 36,893. The Department of National Defence budget provides for a military personnel payroll of $2,168 billion or 31 per cent of the total budget. The civilian payroll is $834 million, or 12 per cent of the total. Operating costs are $1,789 billion. The capital cost program for the department is $1,511 billion. Grants for contributions come to $196 million. Statutory government contributions to benefit plans amount to $543 million, for a total budget in 1982-83 of $7,041 million.
This year's budget represents a 19.6 per cent increase over lat year's budget. During the 1983-84 and 1984-85 fiscal years, the budget for national defence in Canada will increase by 37 per cent over those two years. The department is quite confident that it will be able to live up to the 3 per cent commitment that NATO ministers agreed to and that their home governments agreed to some time ago. That is a real increase in budget in terms of new equipment for NATO forces.
There has been considerable speculation with regard to the announced reduction in departmental spending estimates of $100 million over each of the next two years. I would like to repeat what the Minister of National Defence said last week on this subject. The reduction of $100 million per year will not be a loss to DND in strict terms. More to the point, there will be a saving. This year the DND budget is 7.041 billion. Included in this was a projected 13 per cent increase for military pay. The final agreement with Treasury Board that was negotiated ended up at an 11 per cent increase. Therefore, there will be a 2 per cent savings which amounts to some $40 million. Next year the military will be held to a 6 per cent increase and 5 per cent the following year, as outlined by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Therefore, the savings to DND will be in the area of $120 million to $140 million each year based on the fact that there is a saving of about $20 million for every 1 per cent increase in pay allocation. There will be no negative impact on any of the department's operational, maintenance or personnel requirements and none of the current capital euqipment programs referred to already will be affected.
The main thrust of the June 28 budget of the Minister of Finance is to reduce inflationary pressures. The Department of National Defence and the Canadian military have accepted

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
their share of the collective Canadian burden. As they demonstrate their commitment to the economic battle ahead, I hope that other Canadian employers will follow suit so that it will be fair to all.
Before leaving the subject of defence, I would like to mention the work of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence during recent months, especially the excellent report on the reserves in Canada. Reserve allocations were again increased this year and improvements to equipment and support for our reserve units are proceeding. Improvements, however, must be made in concert with our over-all defence needs and the question in this regard is not simply one of funding, even though implementation of the major recommendations of the committee would require fairly large doses of additional funds to be allocated to defence. It is rather a question of how Canada, as a member of the North Atlantic Alliance, is to respond to the still emerging security requirements of a changing and far from encouraging strategic setting. I am encouraged that we will meet this challenge and the government will continue to provide the defence department with the resources to do so.
There is one item I want to mention before I close the subject. It is a matter which I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). It concerns the fact that members of the armed forces can be posted in Canada for 10 or 12 years and then suddenly be posted overseas. The member's spouse may have been in the labour market for the course of those years, but the moment the spouse leaves Canada to be with the partner overseas they have no claim for unemployment insurance benefits whatsoever. There should at least be an adjustment payment to such people when they leave the country. This is because their chances of employment at the locations they are going to are very slim indeed. As I said before, the Minister of Finance mentioned in his previous budget that the 3 per cent real increase in the NATO budget, our contribution to NATO as agreed to by NATO defence ministers and their respective governments, will be met.
I now want to turn to how farmers benefit from the budget of June 28. The budget provides numerous measures of interest to farmers, including financial assistance, investment incentives and other measures which will benefit farmers through their effect on the economy. Special farm financial assistance is a new loan program under the Farm Credit Corporation which provides $100 million in 1982-83, and a further $100 million in 1984-85 for farmers in financial distress. Through an interest rate rebate these loans, which should benefit some 1,600 to 1,800 farmers, will be provided at four percentage points below the regular FCC lending rate in those first two years.
The small business investment grant is an interest subsidy program for both incorporated and unincorporated small businesses, including farms, and it provides $400 million over two years to reduce interest costs by up to four percentage
points on loans for new investment. The loans are limited to $500,000 and exclude financing of land, leased property and automobiles. Subject to such limitations, loans under the Farm Credit Corporation could qualify.
The small business bond program, introduced in the November, 1981 budget, is continued in its present form to refinance small businesses, including farms in financial difficulty. The taxation of investment income and interest rates is an important subject. Proposals have been made to reduce the taxation of the inflationary component of interest income and capital gains earned on new investments. Such approaches, if implemented, would reduce the cost of borrowing to farmers and other small businessmen as well as home buyers. The 12.5 per cent tax on dividends paid by small corporations, including farm corporations, is postponed to January, 1983 and clarification is provided on the application of the reserve and forward averaging provisions.
The general thrust of the budget is to bring down inflation by wage and price restraint and stimulate investment and job creation while containing the deficit. This will hopefully help economic recovery, and thus the prosperity of agriculture. When agriculture does not prosper, neither does the implement dealer, nor the car dealer, nor the small business operator in that area. There are many offshoots.
How many farms will be assisted by the $100 million provided to the Farm Credit Corporation in the June 28 budget? The program is expected to last for a period of two years with loan approvals of $100 million expected in 1982-83 and $100 million in 1983-84. This should assist about 700 farmers. What are the benefits of the program to the farmer? The farmer receives an interest rebate of four percentage points for two years to reduce his effective cost of credit. Loans approved under the FCC's current interest rate of 16.5 per cent would actually cost the farmer 12.5 per cent for two years.
On the matter of the road to recovery, in these times of international, political and economic instability, we as Canadians must face harsh realities. We must all join in to fight inflation, to boost confidence, to take steps to create jobs and to deal squarely with the deficit. The government has outlined a viable and functional program of recovery. It has set specific guidelines to deal with every facet of the economy, both short term and long term. As I said initially, those short-term policies must be flexible and the government and the Minister of Finance must be prepared to change if the long-term goals are not seen in the light in which they should be seen. Cooperation is the keynote of this schedule of recovery and only co-operation will lead to its successful implementation.
Canadians have responded positively to many other emergencies or crises in the past and I have faith that they will do so again as long as they perceive that all is being done fairly, and this word is the key. The government has identified factors which have combined to make Canadian businesses reluctant to expand. They include idle capacity of equipment, falling profits, heavy interest costs and expanding debt.
July 6, 1982

In order to boost confidence in the marketplace, the government has presented the following proposals: Canadians investing funds in a new form of term deposit would not be taxed on that part of interest which reflects only the rate of inflation. Canadians investing funds in new plans for purchase of common shares of Canadian corporations would not be taxed on that part of the capital gain on such shares that reflect only inflation.
I have others listed which 1 would like to put on the record, but I see that my allotted time has expired, and I want to thank hon. members of this House for their attention.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which provides the launching pad for this debate was introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in the following words:
That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government.
The minister then proceeded with a litany of serious and growing problems confronting the people of Canada, which 1 believe have resulted in large measure from the government's ill-conceived economic policy over the past number of years. He was absolutely right in stating:
Canadians want to know how we can get our economy growing again, how we can get industry to invest, expand and provide the jobs our people need. A million

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
two hundred thousand among us are unemployed. Still more are struggling to make ends meet in the face of high inflation and high interest rates. We are still suffering, one way or another, from the recession that is battering our economy. We are all searching for a way out of it.
The minister's gloomy assessment is certainly well-founded. As one scans the picture of the past few months of this year, it will be noted that every indicator underlines the serious condition in which we find ourselves, and predictions for the future are anything but encouraging. The Canadian economy is in a tailspin. The gross national product fell by 2 per cent in the first quarter, the third consecutive quarter of negative growth, and the largest quarterly decline in 28 years. The Statistics Canada leading indicator has fallen for nine consecutive months. Corporate profits in the first quarter of 1982 were only 41 per cent of the level recorded in the same period in 1981. Manufacturing output in the first quarter of 1982 was only at 70 per cent of capacity-the lowest level of capacity utilization since records were first kept in 1961.
The transportation industry was operating only at 51 per cent of capacity. According to the Conference Board, consumer confidence is at the lowest level in the 20 year history of the consumer attitude index. Business confidence is at the lowest level in the five-year history of the business opinion service. In the past five months of 1982, 4,429 businesses have declared bankruptcy-up 36 per cent from the same period in 1981, and up 55 per cent from the same period in 1980. Farm bankruptcies are up by 61 per cent from last year's level and up 111 per cent from 1980. The unemployment rate in May was 10.2 per cent. A record 1,241,000 Canadians were unemployed. I believe that in effect it was greater than that. There has been a net loss of 320,000 jobs since August and 157,000 in manufacturing alone.
This would indicate, Mr. Speaker, that the minister's gloomy statement has been very well proven. Of course, when the members of the opposition are charged with being prophets of gloom, then, I guess, that will have to tie in the Minister of Finance as well, because that was the statement, those were the indications, that he gave to us in the outline that I present.
Interest rates have started to climb again as the government attempts to support the dollar. The chartered banks' prime rate is now 18.25 per cent compared to 16.5 per cent in the United States. At the time of the 1980 election, the Canadian chartered bank prime rate was 14.75 per cent. Ten years ago, it was 6 per cent. Consumer prices in 1982 were 11.8 per cent higher than in 1981. In contrast, the United States inflation rate is only 6.7 per cent. The main factors behind the May inflation rate were housing, up 13.4 per cent, and transportation up 16.1 per cent on a year over year basis. On a month to month basis, meat prices were 7.5 per cent higher in May than in April. The Canadian dollar is trading for about 78 cents, U.S., and has been as low as 76.86, U.S., in recent days. In October, 1976, the dollar was worth $1.03 U.S. At the time of the November budget the dollar was worth 0.85 U.S.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me continue to support the statement of the minister. I would not like to disappoint him and take exception to what he said, because these figures do point out
the very serious condition that the minister outlined in his introductory presentation.
Since the election, gasoline prices have risen by 86 cents per gallon. Since the October, 1980 budget, 270 drilling and service rigs, worth a total of $1.1 billion, have left Canada. The Alsands project was shelved. The recession has made a shambles of the spending and revenue forecast made in the November budget. Spending will be more than the forecast $75.5 billion and revenues will be significantly less than the forecast $65 billion. As a consequence, Mr. Speaker, it is expected that the deficit originally forecast to be $10.5 billion this year will be somewhere in the range of $18 to $20 billion, and possibly higher.
This is the picture, Mr. Speaker, that has brought us to the present time. This is the backdrop to the picture and the presentation that the minister made just a few nights ago. Now, what are the projections for the future? In November, the Minister of Finance told us that in 1982 there would be real growth in the economy of 2.2 per cent, that the unemployment rate would be 7.8 per cent and that inflation would rise to 11.7 per cent. Now, less than seven months later, he tells us that we will have to endure a drop in the real gross national product of 2 per cent-the worst record of any OECD country-that the unemployment rate will be 10 per cent and that despite the oil glut and lower than expected food prices, inflation will remain at 11 per cent. The projected negative growth rate of the economy, minus 2 per cent, is the worst since 1962.
The government does not tell the Canadian people or the financial markets what it dares to project for the future. This is the same Minister of Finance who told us that between the second quarter of 1981 and the second quarter of 1982 real output would increase by about 1.5 per cent, yet during the first months of that period it had fallen 4 per cent.
I could go on with this litany of problems and the steps downward and backward as far as the economy is concerned, but I do not think it is necessary to do so at the present time. Those Canadians who have been speaking out regarding the budget provisions have been very disappointed and very pessimistic. Articles appearing in foreign periodicals have also indicated that there is little hope for the Canadian economy.
On the evening of Monday, June 28 the minister brought down another budget which failed dismally to present any policy that will in any way solve our major problems.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Disaster.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps some of the provisions in the budget have some value, but in the over-all picture it is difficult to understand how the minister has the gall to ask the House to approve in general the budgetary policies of the government when the response from the public is that the budget is a compounding of our problems rather than a cure and when the answers to questions directed to the government are devoid of any real hope and confidence.
July 6, 1982

I would like to place on the record one or two statements which have appeared in newspapers. An article in the Ottawa Citizen of July 3 states that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has backed off from its initial acceptance of the federal budget by saying that the measures introduced will not bring down inflation or boost sagging investor confidence. The chamber also repeated the statement made by the president that the chamber is concerned about the anticipated $19.6 billion deficit this coming year. The article says that the magnitude of the deficit is alarming and that the mere existence of such a large deficit will continue to fuel inflationary expectations and erode investor confidence. That was one statement. Mr. Charles Lynch, who is rather well known in media circles, stated that it now seems clear that the budget is two and a half years ahead of its time and that the Minister of Finance is trying to catch up, having fiddled while the economy was burning and the deficit was eating up everything in sight.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Brutal, brutal government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't listen to the guy behind you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I heard a comment. I am not quite sure what was said.
As I said, many commentators have expressed the very same views and launched the same criticisms regarding the present budget as those which were launched against the budget of last November.
As I indicated, there are several components of this budget which warrant some degree of support. Such components are retraining programs and assistance to home owners, small business, agriculture, fisheries and so forth. These are good, but in the over-all picture they will do little to ease the feeling of disillusionment and distrust with which Canadians view the policies and actions of this government. I say there is some degree of support, but a close analysis of even the seemingly more worthwhile proposals demonstrates that they are so fraught with uncertainty and vagueness that even now the result is skepticism and anger across the nation.
We all remember that the leader of my party appointed a task force to go across the country and give the people an opportunity to express their views in connection with the previous budget. Of course, to a large extent the philosophy of the previous budget and also many of the policies of the government are being carried on with the present budget. The people who appeared before our task force came to some conclusions, and one of them was that the November budget- and I say possibly the present budget-was completely inappropriate for the then current state of the economy, and indicated clearly that the government had embarked on a course designed to remove incentives for the achievement of economic and social goals from the taxation system and to replace them with direct government grants and subsidies. It seems to me that the direction in which we are going is to make everybody more and more dependent upon government not only for their livelihood through being employed by
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
governments but also through being dependent upon governments for those assistance programs of which they are desperately in need because of the economic conditions in which we find ourselves.
In the course of the hearings of our task force certain individuals and groups requested that their identities be not revealed because they were afraid grants or contracts would not be forthcoming. Although they were critical of the government, they said, "We have to work with these fellows." They also pointed out that in connection with applications under various programs they were afraid their applications would be denied because of the criticism they were launching. Is this the kind of society we want in Canada? Are our people to be brought to heel by the fear that the political system might be used to destroy them unless they bow submissively at the feet of a dictatorial government? There is real fear across the country that our society will become so regimented, regulated and dominated by government that political and economic freedoms will soon be things of the past.
I mentioned the fact that some views were gleaned at the hearings held by the task force. The task force listened to Canadians expressing their views on the situation with which they were confronted. There was and is a growing feeling that the government has closed its ears to the voice of the people and has closed its ears to the needs of the various areas of the country. This committee provided a vehicle by which citizens could be heard and their views on the November 1981 budget considered. I want to tie all that in with the budget that is now before us which, while it gives assistance to a few people in several different sectors, does absolutely nothing to meet the challenge of the major problems facing the country at the present time which are making the programs which the government has proposed necessary.
The spokesmen for the government have said a number of times, and it was repeated by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) today, that they have never heard a positive suggestion come from members on this side of the House. Someone across the aisle says that that is right, Mr. Speaker, but that must be someone who is not often in the House.
Just the other day the leader of this party outlined some of the basic principles that would be necessary if we are to turn the economy around. Certainly this is what the Minister of Finance said must be done-that we have to change and improve conditions, that we have to improve employment and investment and a lot of other things. My leader stated categorically what the steps and the important principles were that must be underlined in any program to achieve these objectives.
Apparently hon. members opposite who are chiming in today did not hear the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) when he spoke the other day and presented some of the changes that would be brought in under the direction of a Progressive Conservative government. I will enumerate some of them. We would eliminate the provisions of

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
the November budget. The Minister of Finance has not done this; he has skirted around it and changed certain things. What he should have done was to say that the budget was a disaster, as the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) said, and that it is to be changed and the government will start all over again.
The hon. member for Mississauga South said that if we were the government we would change the National Energy Program, and he outlined some of those changes. This is one of the things that has caused havoc in the business community of the nation. It has brought untold hardship and unemployment to thousands of workers; it has scared off investment and has been a disaster in total. My colleague also said that we would attack government spending and that an all-party committee would be appointed to consider priorities in government spending. He enumerated some of the things that are in question and suggested the elimination of the capital gains tax and of many other things.
I suggest that we on this side of the House have made many positive suggestions to the government, but it has not listened. Once in a while it takes up one of our suggestions and brings it forward in another guise but it has not repudiated this disastrous budget although my leader and my colleagues have pointed out what should be done to bring about a readjustment in the economy.
One of the recommendations of this committee of which I spoke was to restore individual and investor confidence by establishing a climate for careful development and expansion. This recommendation was the result of discussions held across the nation. Another recommendation was that we should get moving with major projects to stimulate the economy, to create jobs and to meet urgent national and regional needs. It was recommended that the November 12 budget be withdrawn and replaced with an economic plan to provide job creation and economic development to the private sector. Instead of that, the government depends more and more upon the public sector to bring people under its control where they are robbed of the opportunity of making their own decisions and living their own lives.
Now the government asks what should be done? The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) pleaded with the opposition to help the government. Time and time again the government says that we must work together to beat the demons of inflation and unemployment. In November of 1979 it never thought of co-operation or working together. It had only one thing on its mind and that was to get back into office. Now it is back and it pleads for us to work together for the good of the nation. I wish there was more consistency in the government benches.
The government has failed to keep its promises to wrestle inflation to the ground, to beat unemployment, to bring interest rates down and to introduce equity and fairness in taxation and housing. It has failed, Mr. Speaker. A few changes have been made, but nothing substantial enough to meet the challenge.
The minister lacks confidence in his own declaration to the extent that he would not make any projections in his budget. He was ashamed to do that because he has been wrong so often and did not want to risk being wrong again.
The policies of the government have been disastrous and there is no confidence in the economy, in the government or in our ability to pull ourselves up. That has been reflected in the value of the Canadian dollar. The government is borrowing billions of dollars to try to bolster our dollar. Surely there is a positive way to meet these challenges and solve national problems, that is through the competent management of our affairs that Canadians have a right to expect.
This government cannot do it, so it should resign and let someone else take over.
