subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just cannot refuse the thunderous applause which invites me to speak. You were correct, Mr. Speaker, when you said the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson) had just finished speaking at the break. He quoted a number of facts and figures, which I agree with for the most part. If I may say so, there are a few things which merit our looking at as members and, hopefully with our eyes open, as Canadians. I say that in the hope that the debate tonight will not be as partisan as it was earlier and that we can look at some of the problems and some of the solutions we on this side have to offer.
Today in Canada, Mr. Speaker, over 1.2 million Canadians are without jobs. That is a fact. Throughout the industrial world some 30 million people are unemployed. These numbers are not mere statistics. Each of them represents a personal tragedy of immense human costs.
About three months ago I had the occasion to speak to an audience at Centennial High School in Welland. There a young gentleman, who was the leader of a group called Coalition of the Unemployed, said, "Look at us, we are not mere statistics. We are humans. We have families. We want to
July 6, 1982

work." I believe that this young gentleman was saying precisely what the 1.2 million unemployed Canadians would be saying if they were here.
Earlier this month the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) attended the economic summit with the other leaders of the leading industrial nations of the free world. At the Versailles Summit, the Prime Minister used the word "crisis" to describe the state of the world's economy. Surely that description is no exaggeration. All of our summit partners hope for a recovery. All of the leaders came away from Versailles determined to work within their own countries for that recovery. But they left with little assurance that there will be the kind of concerted economic action the world situation so desperately demands. Realizing that the beginning of recovery would therefore be further delayed, the Government of Canada concluded that it must act, and it must act at once. To that end a new budget has been brought down.
The Prime Minister, just last Wednesday, asked all the premiers to join as full partners in the battle for economic renewal.
The road back to recovery must begin with a realistic assessment of what this country can control and what we cannot control. Canada cannot deal with its economic problems in isolation; we can ease, if not eliminate, the impact of some problems, but the solutions to other difficulties depend on events beyond our borders. I do not think there are many members here who would disagree with these statements. We must know what we can realistically change and what is beyond our power to change by ourselves.
Canada is a trading nation. If our partners are suffering from a worldwide recession, then the international market for our products will be weak. That is an economic fact of life we cannot change by ourselves.
Canada is a resource exporting nation, and commodity prices have experienced their steepest decline in decades. At 58 cents a pound, for example, copper is at its lowest price since the 1930s. Lead, zinc and other minerals are not far behind. There is little that the government can do about the fall in worldwide commodity prices.
Finally, interest rates in the United States are hurting the whole world economy, and that is what the Prime Minister told President Reagan at Versailles. We all know that. The Canadian dollar, like every other western currency, is captive to the extraordinarily high real rate of interest in the U.S. These are the hard realities of a worldwide economic interdependence.
Yet, while recognizing the force of world conditions, we must acknowledge too that many of our problems originate here at home. Our inflation rate of 11.8 per cent is far too high. Our cost structure is becoming prohibitively expensive. To put it simply, we are pricing ourselves out of world markets. We are losing our competitive edge. All this we have done to ourselves. And what we have done, we can reverse.
I believe that expectations are at the heart of our inflation problem. In the past decade, it was natural for us to believe
The Budget-Mr. Parent
that our prosperity would continue to spiral upwards. We never questioned the roots of our prosperity. We did not look at the world situation and our impending vulnerability, but once again Canada is a trading nation and is affected by the ups and downs of the world economy. For a long while, a few Canadians-the poor, the aged, the helpless, the weakest, paid the price of those inflationary demands. Today only a few groups can pursue their expectations-the powerful, the protected and the privileged. It is the many who pay the cost in unemployment, in bankruptcy and in lost opportunity, not the few I have mentioned.
The charge of having excessive expectations can no longer be laid at the door of the unemployed logger in B.C., the struggling small-business man in Welland or the young homeowner renewing his mortgage in Newfoundland. The expectations of the 1.2 million unemployed have certainly been shattered.
To overcome the twin problems of uncertainty abroad and recession at home, the government has introduced an economic recovery plan in Parliament. We do not believe that everyone in the House is going to agree with it, but we do hope that all members will consider what we have put forward before passing final judgment on it. Three principles are central to that plan. These principles formed the foundation of the budget and the proposals the Prime Minister made to the premiers.
Our first principle is that every Canadian must play his or her part. To deal with our economic difficulties we need the support and co-operation of all. Government can provide leadership, but it is only through the individual decisions of many thousands of Canadians that progress will be made.
It is in times of national challenge and crisis that the mettle and magnitude of our national will is truly tested. I respectfully suggest that this is such a time.
Our second principle is that if we all have a stake in the outcome, we all must share in the effort, each according to his or her ability. Canadians are willing to make sacrifices so that others can be helped. Nobody wants to see his neighbour without a job, nor does any Canadian want to see his neighbour without hope and confidence for surely herein lies the greatest sickness, the greatest disease, because when a nation is without hope and without confidence it atrophies. It pulls back and it is unwilling to reach out to help those who cannot help themselves. We must ask those who are secure to help those who are not as secure. We must ask those who are working to assist the jobless. We must continue to protect the weak, the aged and the helpless. That is a commitment of the Government of Canada. I dare say that that is a commitment of every Member of Parliament who has been elected to come here and represent his or her constituents. But more than that, the commitment of the Government of Canada is a fundamental tenet of our society. We will not fight our economic problems at the expense of the aged, the poor or the unemployed. That would not be right. That would not be acceptable to us as Canadians.

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Parent
Our third principle is the firm conviction that if we have the will we can win this battle. It would be naive, even dangerous, to try to pretend that we are experiencing only a minor disruption. We are in a deep recession. We are in a crisis, as was stated by the Prime Minister at Versailles. But it would be equally wrong and equally dangerous to throw up our hands and say that all is lost, that we must sit helplessly by while inflation rages and unemployment grows. Despite our problems and despite all of the setbacks that we face now as a nation, Canada remains a land more blessed than most. It is true that it is probably in vogue today to knock one another here in the House. It is probably in vogue to try to dwell upon our ills. But in dwelling upon our ills we feed the sickness inside of us which says, "We cannot do anything." I for one, and I am sure many other members here, totally discard that assumption.
If we, Canadians, worked together, we could do more than simply preserve our economy. We could turn it around to upward growth. The three principles of responsibility, sharing and hope shaped the budget message. In it we proposed a four-part action plan designed, first, to bring inflation down to at least 6 per cent through a nationwide collective effort; second, to reduce the impact of high interest rates, especially for home owners, small-business men and farmers; third, to create over
300,000	jobs through direct government action and indirectly through improvements in the investment climate; fourth, to maintain the integrity of our social security system. The immediate objective of our society must be to cut inflation nearly in half, down to 6 per cent. We must move, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said, from 12 per cent inflation to 6 per cent recovery. This seems reasonable, and the Government of Canada will lead the way by limiting to 6 per cent the indexing of income taxes and social programs such as family allowances.
With regard to income taxes, it should be noted that this is the first time since 1974 that there have been any increases in personal income taxes. Also, the Government of Canada will lead the way by cutting the salary increases of cabinet ministers and of Members of Parliament from 11 per cent to 6 per cent. I am talking about a cut, I am not talking about a freeze. That is in place now and will continue for the rest of the year. We will do this cutting while limiting the annual increase in public service pensions to the same figure. We know that these are drastic measures, but these measures must be taken.
Also, we will lead the way by ensuring that public service pay increases rise by no more than 6 per cent. It must be said that we realize public servants will be making a sacrifice. We acknowledge that sacrifice by them, but it does not in any way take away from the fact that they are doing good work for Canadians. That we ask them to share with us in carrying the burden is normal. They are at the forefront of the battle, as we are here in the House.
Finally, we will lead the way by holding regulated prices under federal jurisdiction to a 6 per cent increase. Through measures such as limiting the indexation of the tax system,
every taxpayer will be making a contribution to the inflation fight. If the 6 per cent figure we have imposed throughout the federal government becomes the norm in Canada, we will have made a great stride in restoring our international competitiveness.
The second part of our recovery plan is to provide relief from high interest rates. Again I refer to the meeting which I attended where groups representing ten different unions presented briefs at Centennial High School in Welland. The point stressed by all of them again and again-and especially by the Welland and District Labour Council-was that we must bring down interest rates. We must control interest rates or, in the end, they will control us; they will run our lives rather than our controlling them. Alexandre Dumas said in one of his speeches:

He said that like anything else, money is a good servant but a bad master. The same applies here to interest rates. If we let interest rates become our master, we are going to be the servants, we will lose our independence and finally, we will lose everything we have in this beloved country of ours, Canada.

A new and innovative indexed bond instrument will cut interest rates from between 3 per cent to 6 per cent for home owners, farmers, fishermen, small businessmen, home purchasers and investors in Canadian equities. To ensure that this major proposal is implemented properly, consultations will begin immediately with the private sector, and to bridge the gap until this measure becomes law, the Government of Canada will make available grants of up to $3,000 to help home owners with mortgage renewals costing more than 30 per cent of their income. The Government of Canada will now give relief to small business by reducing its borrowing rate by 4 per cent. Also it will provide more assistance for Canadian farmers by reducing their interest rate by 4 per cent through the Farm Credit Corporation.
I should like to quote from a news release of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce concerning Canadian small businesses. It reads:
Small businesses in Canada will benefit greatly as a result of Monday's budget . . . "The new budget has measures for dealing with the specific needs of Canada's small businesses"-
How will we do this? We will do it with reduced interest rate costs. It continues:
Direct grants will be made available to small businesses over the next two years to cover 4 per cent of interest costs on depreciable property, research and development. Incorporated and unincorporated small businesses as well as farmers and fishermen are eligible.
This new $400 million small business investment grant program is in addition to the ongoing small business bond program which provides interest relief in cases of financial difficulty.
Direct employment and economic programs will receive half a billion dollars of new money to provide jobs for Canadians. Of this $500 million, $300 million will expand programs such as the Enterprise Development Program, the Defence Industry Productivity Program, the Regional Fund, and the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program.
July 6, 1982

My riding of Welland has benefited on three different occasions by way of the industry and labour adjustment program. Many in Canada's small business community will benefit as Canadians move to take advantage of the new five-point housing package which was announced. Building trades will receive a major boost as housing programs begin to generate some 65,000 new jobs over the next two years. An additional 54,000 jobs are expected from the Canada rental support plan for the construction of new rental units. In total,
119.000	new jobs are expected. But perhaps what is the most exciting are the potential measures we will be taking to help small businesses and home owners.
The Minister of Finance tabled a consultative document containing proposals which, if implemented, would have the following effects. Canadians investing funds in a new form of term deposit would not be taxed on that part of interest which only reflects the rate of inflation. Canadians investing funds in new plans for the purchase of common shares of Canadian corporations would not be taxed on that part of the capital gain or on shares that only reflect inflation. Buyers of new homes will be able to secure mortgages from 3 per cent to 6 per cent below prevailing rates. Small businesses, farmers and fishermen will be able to secure loans for new capital investment at similarly reduced interest rates.
We are determined-and when I say "we" I mean hon. members on both sides of the House-to lower interest rates in the long term and to reduce their present impact upon the groups affected most. Lowering inflation and lessening the impact of interest rates will start the process of economic recovery, but to create the jobs Canada needs we must do even more. In my opinion jobs must come first. To that end we have ordered government departments to cut and reallocate their spending so that money can be freed for job creation. We will not add to the deficit through these measures, but the reallocation will be substantial. Our goal is to create more than
300.000	jobs over two years, many of them in the construction industry. We want this country to start building again. Through measures introduced this spring as well as in the budget our programs will create 150,000 jobs in the housing industry. Our goal is to put this country back to work.
Last week we protected our system of social benefits. Lower and middle-income Canadians who would lose because of cuts in family allowance indexation will gain a $50 increase in the child tax credit. For families making less than $25,000 a year there will be no loss of income. Similarly, those senior citizens who are receiving the guaranteed income supplement, the GIS, to the old age pension, will not have their benefits cut in any way. That point must be noted and repeated again and again so that we do not foster this type of anxiety among our pensioners. Indeed, the GIS will be fully indexed to the rate of inflation.
Our program of action does not end with consultation with the provinces. In the weeks ahead the Minister of Finance and
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
other ministers will ask leaders of business and labour to meet. Specific proposals will be made to them. As well, specific plans will be put before them. It is clear that we do not seek to use these discussions to identify culprits, to attach blame or to single out groups in Canada to bear the burden. Enough of that. We have had enough of trying to put the finger on someone else.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who is it?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely we should look at ourselves. The hon. member thinks that it is funny enough to make jokes when we have 1.2 million unemployed in Canada. I do not think it is a joke.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is your fault.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have all been touched by economic adversity. Even the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) who is the one who dares to make jokes on such a situation should realize that we have all been hurt. We are hurting now. If we do not act together, we will hurt more.
The interest of organized labour is the wellbeing of Canadian working men and women. That must be our interest also. The interest of business is the willingness of the investor to put his money to productive use in Canada. That is our interest as well.
Surely when factories are closing, when jobs are disappearing, when worldwide recession has reduced our export sales, individual Canadians should be able to rely on the leaders of the great institutions in their society to act together. I call upon all members here to do just that.
That is the message and the challenge we bring to Canadians. It is a message of hope and a challenge to share. We are confident that we can overcome our difficulties and return to better times.
Canada is like a family. In a time of personal tragedy the family can join together, stay together and either solve their problems or fall apart. This, then, is a challenge to us all as Canadians, to share in the sacrifices and join in the collective effort that will turn our goals into realities.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hasten to take part in this debate which we owe to the government's bringing down its third budget in a matter of months, and 1 also hasten to comment on the remarks made by the member for Welland (Mr. Parent) before he sat down, when he implied that the member for Joliette was joking when he asked a simple question. Mr. Speaker, he said we should not try to find the culprit. I think we have every reason to ask who is responsible for this tragic situation. In fact, the hon. member admits the situation exists and that we are in the middle of a serious recession. He said, and it is perhaps the ultimate paradox I have heard in these several days of budget debate: when a nation is without hope and without confidence, it atrophies.

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
Unfortunately, the member for Welland fails to realize that he is one of the members of the team that put us in this situation in the first place. He also pointed out that after 15 years, the time has come to build this country. After 15 years, Mr. Speaker, I have heard and seen quite a bit in my time here in the House, and I am one of those Canadians who have deplored in every possible way the situation we happen to find ourselves in at the present time. And now members on the government side are telling us today that they are determined to put Canada on the road to progress!
How can Canadians as a whole believe such a statement when the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has shown such unprecedented incompetence? How can the Minister of Finance, who was speaking about a deficit of about $9 to $10 million two or three months ago, confess publicly-and I can understand how embarrassing this must have been-this monumental deficit which quite legitimately frightens Canadian businessmen? Mr. Speaker, I have been sitting in this House for 15 years, if we exclude the few weeks when I was absent because I had the courage to offer something and to share the problems which were affecting all of Quebec. Nearly all businessmen and editorial writers consider this new budget the disaster of the century. I could quote a series of articles written by various English-speaking and French-speaking editorial writers. Everyone agrees on this point. The Canadian Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is worsening the crisis of confidence and the new budget can only lead the country to depression and disaster. This is the type of comment made by nearly all editorial writers, and I find this rather exceptional.
1 believe that it is important to note that Mr. Ivan Guay wrote in La Presse:
The federal Minister of Finance, Mr. Allan McEachen, confirmed the predictions of all serious observers. He remained true to himself by bringing down a third budget which does not take our economy out of the rut where his two previous budgets have put it. He has indeed confirmed this-
To understand the situation, Mr. MacEachen did not bring down a new budget seven and a half months after the previous one to change the economic policy of his government, but rather to change the image of his government, which has been accused of a lack of leadership and whose credibility is rapidly going downhill. He has therefore attempted to give the people new confidence in his government and at the same time in the economy. However, as could be expected, he has failed on both counts.
Why do politicians keep on telling people just about anything as though we were all morons?
These are some of the comments made by this editorial writer about this government. He also adds, and I quote:
The federal government will inject $2.3 billion in the economy, but will take back $3 billion from your pockets.
This is the type of hypocrisy we are now witnessing. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. Parent) and many others are asking us to cooperate. In his budget, the Minister of Finance talked of sharing and said that the time had come to share the concerns and the problems of this government, this same government which has put the country in the situation we are now facing. The Minister of Finance asked us to share his
mistakes and his incompetence! This is too much, Mr. Speaker! I do not believe that the Canadian people would respect us or allow us-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or forgive us-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-or forgive us if we were to cooperate with a government which has shown such incompetence in the last 15 years, and especially in the last three. Mr. Speaker, this debate on a second budget in less than six months is justified by the unprecedented failure of this government. The residents of the Joliette constituency are worried too and they live in a climate of uncertainty.
I share their concern, of course, and I submit that this government's wrong decisions, especially these last three years, have led Canada to bankruptcy. While the Canadian people was being deceived with constitutional reform, which anyway satisfies nobody and for Quebecers is a source of genuine indignation, the government, following the instructions of the current Minister of Finance, had deficits on top of deficits and increased government expenditures at staggering rates. Of course this put Canada in the situation we now have, the worst recession this country has ever known. And this with the complicity of his colleagues, including the Right Hon. Prime Minister and at least six dozen members from my province, and almost as many from outside. Being too weak to get the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister out of their errors, they preferred through their weakness to share the errors of that government that led Canada into our current difficulties.
Not so long ago, Mr. Speaker, and it is important that Canadians remember this, this Prime Minister in his own province was boasting everywhere of the beauty of the land, its potential for development thanks to its territories and their resources.
How is it, Mr. Speaker, that those legitimate hopes faded so quickly? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker. From the solemn commitment of this Prime Minister in 1968 to a just society until the principle of fairness promised by the Minister of Finance in November last, is there any other term for this government than impostor in the current situation? Arrogance and hypocrisy replace co-operation between the provincial partners and compassion for this country's citizens.
I referred to the government's wrong choices over these last three years. I am thinking for instance of the government's excessive involvement in the energy area. The socializing attitude deep down in the Prime Minister's heart for more than 35 years was espoused by his party, unwittingly of course, because they are implementing the policies of the New Democratic Party which the Prime Minister was supporting before he joined the Liberal ranks. That government intervention, Mr. Speaker, equates to the loss of the megaprojects, which is
July 6, 1982

tremendously costly to Canada at this point, which cost billions of dollars of investments and the loss of thousands of jobs, with the direct complicity of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). And they say they are capable of re-establishing a climate that is favourable to investment. The proof is there, Mr. Speaker. Those people have no respect whatsoever for free enterprise. By refusing to so admit publicly, they are forcing even the New Democratic Party to vote against the budget. I referred to the failure of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It is unbelievable the situation we are in, especially since these last three years. I listened today to the Minister in charge of Housing. He referred to something new, he would have us believe in new hopes, a recovery, when we know perfectly well he is responsible for the current housing situation.
Not so long ago, this government raked us over the coals because we had the intention of promoting the housing sector which is so vitally important for the economic development of our country. This minister is now talking about boosting the construction industry, but he is mainly responsible for the loss of 400,000 jobs in Canada because he refused to act and upgrade the major sector of construction. It is the same minister who even turned down ten of his own colleagues and a few ministers, failing to meet the emergency and to act quickly in that field. I was listening to him today when he spoke with the hyprocrisy which is the hallmark of that group of ministers, trying to raise the hopes of Canadians by telling them that the situation is not really as bad as we describe it. Mr. Speaker, we know full well that if we had primed the construction sector, the small and medium-sized businesses would not be in the mess they are in now. Small and medium-size businesses would have made profits and maintained a large number of jobs if the government had been attuned and had grasped the significance of giving a shot in the arm of the construction industry three years ago. Here again, the minister shirked his responsibilities and he is party to a bankrupt situation the likes of which Canada has never seen.
I heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who keeps on claiming that we have the best agricultural legislation, the best agricultural products and the best agricultural system. How can anyone explain, for instance, that farmers have never been as deep in debt as they have in the past five or six years as a result of policies which call for huge investments and unacceptable interest rates? Never have so many farmers been pushed to the brink of bankruptcy. But the Minister of Agriculture does not say one word about that. I might also refer to the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) who, as I am speaking to you this evening, has yet to solve the issue of shoes and footwear. The footwear industry is still waiting for an answer, but the Minister of State for International Trade makes it cool its heels. Along with his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), he is responsible for the loss of nearly 10,000 jobs in that
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
leading sector and he is still preaching patience to that industry which employs between 10,000 and 15,000 workers and yet does not ask for handouts. It is not a question of going begging, we simply want the government to show respect for an industry which has proven itself and to have some regard for all businesses which operate in Canada.
For a number of months now, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has been announcing programs worth millions of dollars and members opposite keep repeating that the government is investing millions in such and such fields. Why did they let the situation deteriorate to such an extent that the Minister of Employment and Immigration alone will probably have to spend close to $1 million this year? Mr. Speaker, all those programs are just another form of social welfare. They talk about occupational training programs for jobs which exist only on paper, and about retirement pensions at age 50, as if that was the end of life for a man or a woman. That is nothing more and nothing less than hidden welfare. And then, Mr. Speaker, they want us to cooperate and praise the efforts of the Minister of Finance and the appeal that the Prime Minister made to his provincial colleagues last week. How interesting to see the pathetic attitude of the Prime Minister today before the provincial premiers. Having shown such arrogance towards them, he must now ask them and beg them on his knees to be party to his monumental failure.
How is it that the Right Hon. Prime Minister never felt the need to call a meeting of the premiers before this budget was tabled? Is it necessary for the federal government to impose again its will at all cost? And now the Right Hon. Prime Minister, relying on public opinion, feels that the provincial premiers would never dare refuse publicly to work toward the economic recovery of Canada. If so many businessmen, economists and knowledgeable people find it difficult to support this policy it is because they feel such a disastrous budget is not likely to put the economy on the way to recovery. Businessmen in particular and the Canadian people in general cannot depend on promises of this kind from the Liberal Party, because they were disappointed so many times in the past. Under these circumstances, it is clear that most Canadians want a new government. Why? Because this deceitful government is unable to ensure the private sector and free enterprise their proper places. All the Right Hon. Prime Minister has told the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on the role of private enterprise is an unforgivable falsehood. All the economic projections which the Minister of Finance has made were proven entirely wrong. So the Minister of Finance has lost his credibility, something he and all other members on the government's side are perfectly aware of.
I see the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) who is about to tell us once again that we do not know how to read

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
the budget, we do not understand the budget. If there is something that we do understand, however, it is the fact that there were only 300,000 unemployed in Canada 15 years ago, compared with 1,500,000 now. We know also that come December 31, Canadians by the thousands will no longer collect their scanty pittance, or rather, their unemployment insurance benefits. And these ministers have neither the courage nor the honesty to admit it. That is the predicament in which we find ourselves now! And we are being asked to cooperate with such an utterly incompetent government! It is impossible, Mr. Speaker! And if the government is truly convinced that Canadians are willing to trust them after a budget as disastrous as that which was tabled six months ago and another one last week, let them have the decency to go to the people and ask them if they can trust a government which has deceived them so often and so long. Such is our government and we are going to denounce it! The time to do it is right now! I cannot tolerate the hypocrisy of my hon. friends opposite who are perfectly aware of the situation and who feign surprise.
Yesterday and again today, I heard people say: we are indeed in an impossible situation. Should the Canadian people help us? Should the provinces help us? This government is mostly responsible for this abysmal failure. How can this government and the Minister of Finance who have lost their credibility in the eyes of business, create again a climate of trust? It is unthinkable, Mr. Speaker. And these people know that it is unthinkable. They will play with time at the expense of the Canadian people. And they claim they want to help Canadians! These people have destroyed Canada, have split the country with their Constitutional scheme and have placed it in a state of economic dependency. And in a while the Minister of State for Finance will make his little speech, claiming that we do not understand, what it means for thousands and millions of unemployed not to know whether they will be able to find a job tomorrow morning. And the housing minister would like us to believe that with his $3,000 grant, he will get the housing industry moving again, when Canadians can no longer afford to borrow at the current high interest rates. Why did the government deliberately create unemployment? Listen to this one! Last week, the Minister of Finance said in connection with his $20 billion deficit that he had not foreseen that he would be faced with a revenue loss, due to the
1,200,000	unemployed who, with all the others, are about 1,500,000! He had not realized that by deliberately creating unemployment, there would be a loss of income tax and the unemployment insurance fund would be depleted. Yet the Minister of Finance has the nerve to ask members of this House and Canadians in general to trust him. It is a disaster, Mr. Speaker, and his cohorts are supporting and commending him. I think that Canadians must realize the extent of their hypocrisy. Last week, I was surprised to hear the Minister of
Finance announce a reduction in our salaries. Well, of course it is quite fine, because we are showing some leadership. We ask Canadians to tighten their belts while the Minister of Finance is increasing his electoral expenditures by some 20 per cent each year. Now they are going to play the game and reduce the members' salaries with Liberal members applauding Mr. Speaker. It is the height of hypocrisy as though they were pleased and were going to make up the deficit of the Minister of Finance. Of course, if the deficit were made up, we would be delighted, but this will not be the case, Mr. Speaker. Under the circumstances, I have the impression that the time allotted to me is running out, but this government cannot rely on this speaker to support a pitiful budget, such a deplorable administration. I hope that enough members on that side are sufficiently scrupulous and honest to get rid of a minister who is bringing this country to the verge of bankruptcy and to invite Canadians to let us know what kind of government they want. I would like to know as soon as possible if Canadians really want to give their confidence to such a seedy and pitiable team.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his speech, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) referred to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who appealed to the spirit of solidarity of all Canadians, to their willingness to share and to their courage, urging them to work together in a common resolve to get through this recession. However, instead of urging Canadians to join in this common effort, the hon. member prefers to denigrate such appeals and makes cynical remarks instead of taking a responsible view, instead of showing the facts as they are and offering a more balanced picture of the present situation. To hear the hon. member talk, the Canadian government is to blame for the problem being experienced by Western economies. The hon. member for Joliette has quite a reputation for his simplistic analyses, and, true to form, in his speech tonight he showed his usual capacity for logic and his usual simplistic approach to the facts. In any case, I am not going to waste any more time on his rhetoric, and I know Canadians will judge what he said as they judged in the past the way he defended his party's policies.
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes I have been allowed, I intend to discuss a document that was tabled by the Minister of Finance when he made his budget statement, a document that deals with inflation and the taxation of personal investment income. It is a relatively lengthy and complex piece of work, and I shall try to summarize it in simple terms, to give Canadians who may not have had an opportunity to read it for themselves, a general idea of the content and help them understand how these proposals can benefit Canadians by providing mechanisms that will help reduce interest rates.
July 6, 1982

It is widely recognized, Mr. Speaker, that inflation causes a number of distortions in the economy's various markets, distortions which lead to an inappropriate allocation of both financial and human resources and finally are instrumental in slowing down the economy. Although it is not always easy to visualize the real impact of inflation on the economy, we are all aware of the element of uncertainty that inflation has brought into our lives. In the present situation, where we are experiencing galloping inflation, it has become practically impossible to plan medium and long-term financial commitments. In fact, how can we save money for a rainy day, how can we borrow money to buy a house, how can we buy life insurance, if we realize that the value of our dollar is going to be constantly eroded year after year because inflation rates are going to continue at their present high levels or will even increase, so that we no longer know what the dollar we are investing today will be worth in five, ten, fifteen or twenty-five years?
Rising interest rates as a result of inflation can create serious cash-flow problems for borrowers and also disrupt the proper functioning of the financial markets. These problems have become particularly acute at the present time for people buying homes and for small businesses, and are thus contributing to the severity of the present recession. In the housing industry, inflation-related increases in interest rates have caused monthly payments of interest and principal on a mortgage amortized over twenty-five years to rise by 80 to 90 per cent. In the case of a long-term, fixed-rate mortgage, homeowners have to tighten their belts during the first few years and can subsequently benefit from a rapid decline in the real value of monthly payments as a result of the time they have gained. In the more frequent case of short-term mortgages, home owners must live with the fact that they may be faced with a sudden rise in interest rates, and as a result, prospective home buyers postpone the purchase of a first home to avoid this uncertainty and the need to cope with all these problems.
Cash-flow problems are even more serious in the case of businesses which borrow funds at a floating interest rate which subsequently rises due to an unanticipated increase in inflation. They are then required to increase their cash payments to lenders immediately by the full amount of the increase in interest rates, thus leading to serious cash-flow problems which may lead a business to bankruptcy. On the financial markets, the uncertainty caused by inflation makes long-term loans less attractive, both for borrowers and lenders. If inflation is higher than expected, the borrower will gain at the expense of the lender, while if inflation is lower than expected, the lender will gain at the borrower's expense. The effect of this uncertainty is currently seen in the shortening of the term of fixed rate mortgages and other loans and by the increased use of floating-rate term loans. The increase in the proportion of term deposits held in maturities of under one year reflects a similar reluctance for long- and medium-term commitments by
The Budget-Mr. Bussieres
lenders. Finally, the lack of long-term capital has brought about a decline in investment, thus contributing to the general decline in productivity and especially to the erosion of our competitive edge on international markets.
These are some of the reasons, Mr. Speaker, why the government has made a firm resolve to tackle the problem of inflation by announcing its objective in the present budget to bring down the inflation rate to 6 per cent and by appealing to the solidarity of all Canadians and all economic partners to work together to achieve this objective. Inflation also creates more specific problems in the tax system by introducing the distortions I mentioned earlier in the taxation of investment income. During an inflationary period, the investor makes a real profit on an investment only if the total return exceeds compensation for the decline in the real purchasing power of the money which he has invested, a decline in purchasing power as a result of high inflation rates. In fact, the rate of return on an investment could, and can, in fact, be divided into two components. The first component is the real interest that would be paid if there were no inflation, if the inflation rate were nil, and the return on an investment would be a real return, a real interest. The second part, the second element in an investment income is part of the interest or the return equivalent to inflation or compensation for the reduction in the purchasing power of my savings or investments.
In our present system, taxes are levied on both the return ascribable to inflation and the real return which I suggested was the first constituent or the first element of the total return on investments. In our taxation system, all surplus on the first outlay of capital is considered as directly taxable regardless of the reduced real value of the capital, a reduction which is ascribable to inflation. It involves reporting interest income as well as capital gain income and corporate income. The effective increased taxation rates on those incomes discourage savings and investments. In fact, in many cases, not only do investors get no return after taxation but actually lose money. This is what economists call in contradictory terms a rate of negative return. How can we illustrate such a negative yield rate or, to put it in clearer terms, an actual loss on an investment? Let us say, for example, that I have invested $1,000 of my savings at 12 per cent. After one year the investment income would be $120 and if I am in the 35 per cent tax bracket I will have to pay $42 on that $120 income. In other words, the net income on my original investment of $1,000 in savings will be $120 less $42 in taxes, or $78. If inflation is running at 10 per cent, anyone investing $1,000 of his savings will have to earn at least $100 in income if he does not want to lose to inflation, because $1,000 at 10 per cent yields a minimum of $100. So if I want an investment which offsets inflation, I need an income of $100 on an investment of $1,000. In the example I gave earlier, the net income after taxes was $78, therefore an actual loss of $22 for the investor who should get an income of $100 if he wants to keep up with the inflation rate. So he ends up with an actual loss of 2.2 per cent and he is
19076

July 6, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Bussieres
said to have had a negative yield of 2.2 per cent on his investment even though he was given an interest rate of 12 per cent on his SI,000 investment. This difference between real and apparent income causes distortions in the decisions of investors and a rather ineffective allocation of economic and financial resources, which are extremely limited at the present time.
All these problems are considered in the paper for consultation I mentioned earlier which is entitled "Inflation and the Taxation of Personal Investment Income". To eliminate the effects of inflation on the taxation of investment income, this paper proposes two schemes of limited indexation concerning interest income and capital gains to protect the amounts invested or the real investment income of individuals. The first would be the creation of indexed term deposit certificates. These certificates would offer the depositor a tax-free interest on the portion of the investment income which absorbs inflation. These savings would then be made available to homebuy-ers, small-business men, farmers and fishermen, in the form of indexed term loans by the financial institutions offering term deposit certificates. There would therefore be indexed term deposit certificates which would raise funds and provide the depositor with an attractive real return since it would be indexed, and the funds raised would be put at the disposal of the groups I mentioned earlier in the form of indexed term loans.
The second scheme proposed in the paper for consultation would take the form of a new registered shareholder investment plan, under which capital gains on shares purchased for the registered fund would only be taxed on the portion exceeding the rate of inflation. Mr. Speaker, if I may, I would like to take a few minutes to explain and illustrate these two proposed schemes which are now under review. First, I shall deal with the indexed term deposits and term loans which aim at reducing substantially, or up to 6 per cent, the interest rates for potential home owners, small businesses, farmers and fishermen.
What will an indexed term deposit consist of? Canadian financial institutions will be allowed to offer their depositors residing in Canada term deposit certificates for a minimum of one year, which deposit will be indexed. The principal of the term deposit will be adjusted periodically according to CPI variations. Interest will be calculated on the indexed principal at a real rate that would be fixed over the term of the deposit. This rate will be set by each financial institution administering the deposit in the same way as interest rates on conventional term deposits are now set. However, the fact that the deposit itself is indexed will be taken into account. The depositor will be taxed only on the real interest income and only the real interest will be deductible for the financial institution. Since only the real interest, in other words, the interest less the compensation for inflation, will be taxable, this will make the investment yield much more attractive for the depositor.
Moreover, since the financial institution will be able to deduct only real interest, it will be able to minimize its profit margin and reduce the interest offered borrowers on the loans for which the funds raised from these indexed term deposits would be made.
Since only the real interest income would be taxable, the depositor will be able to accept lower interest rates, as I noted earlier. Let us try to visualize or to get a better idea of how this system could work. For instance, let us take an ordinary deposit and a hypothetical inflation rate of 10 per cent. To come back to the situation mentioned earlier, let us take a conventional deposit or savings of $1,000. At the present time, with an interest rate of 16 per cent, the investment or interest income would be $160. Under the Income Tax Act at the present time, the taxable investment income would also be $160. At a tax rate of 40 per cent, the tax payable on this income would be $64, and the net investment income after taxes would therefore be $26. The minimal after-tax rate of return on an amount of $1,000 would therefore be 9.6 per cent and the real after-tax rate of return, if we consider the taxes of $64 to be paid, is of 0.4 per cent plus 0.4 per cent of real yield on a deposit of $ 1,000.
Now, if the deposit were indexed, by how much would my real income increase? I still have the same initial deposit or saving of $1,000. The inflation rate is still 10 per cent. The interest rate on my deposit would be 10 per cent for inflation, in addition to a real interest rate of 2 per cent, for a total of 12 per cent. What would be my income? My interest income would be $1000 to compensate for inflation, since the inflation rate is basically supposed to be 10 per cent, my real interest income would be $20, since the real interest on the $1,000 investment was 2 per cent, the tax to be paid, still with a 40 per cent taxation rate applicable to the $20 of real income, since my real interest is 2 per cent, would be $8, my income after taxes is therefore $1000 to compensate for inflation, 10 per cent of $1,000 in addition to $12 and $20 less $8 of income tax, the real intest income of $20 less $8 would therefore give me an income of $112 after taxes. My nominal return rate after taxes is therefore 11.2 per cent compared to the previous 9.6 per cent and contrary to the previous real return to 4/10 per cent, I will have a real return of 1.2 per cent on the same $1000 investment with that indexation proposal for the term deposit. It can clearly be seen, Mr. Speaker, how the real return on that $1,000 investment when the deposit is indexed to account for inflation allows me to reduce the interest rate on my savings while ensuring me a higher direct return, since the compensatory factor for inflation is subtracted from the amount charged.
So, that system should attract a large number of investors and enable financial institutions to set up a sizeable reserve of funds which they will obtain at low cost, because, as I indicated earlier, instead of paying 16 per cent interest on $1,000, that rate will be reduced to 12 per cent and even though it is
July 6, 1982

lower, the yield will be higher without the compensation for inflation set at 10 per cent for the purposes of our example.
As mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Parent), these funds will be made available to homebuyers, small-business men, farmers and fishermen in the form of term loans. And we now come to the second face of Janus, if I may say so, Mr. Speaker, because these indexed term deposits generate indexed term loans, thereby making money available to lend at interest rates up to 6 percentage points lower than market rates. On an indexed term loan, the real interest rate only would be deductible by the borrower as expense for income tax purposes. The same amount would be taxable in the hands of the lending institution. As in the case of indexed term loans, the initial principal would be adjusted periodically, based on consumer price index variations. Since interest rates are now wholly deductible, the people who will benefit the most from this initiative are firms with very little or no taxable income, and finally home owners who cannot deduct interest rates or loan charges on their mortgages from their taxable income. I would like to attempt once more to illustrate how these loans will be of benefit to all citizens. Assuming that the current interest rate is 19 per cent, the inflation rate 10 per cent and also that financial institutions are ready to lend at a 5 per cent real interest rate, they would have a 3 per cent real margin on the 2 per cent real interest paid on indexed deposits.
Well, for instance, on a loan to a home owner-I do not want to go into the details of loans that could be made to businesses with variable tax rates and I will only deal with home mortgages. To simplify, let us take a SI00 loan. The nominal interest at current market rates would be 19 per cent. The real cost after taxes of the borrowed funds would be $19. Now, let us return to our indexed loan; according to our original hypothesis, the amount of the loan is $100 and the inflation rate is 10 per cent. Included in the interest charged, there is as a first component in the inflation compensation of 10 per cent, as was seen in the previous example, the 5 per cent true interest rate of 5 per cent charged by the lending institution. The after-tax cost of the funds thus borrowed is therefore $15, that is, on $100, the equivalent of 4 per cent lower than the current rates allowed, due to the fact that the term deposit is indexed and that all the moneys collected this way are put again on the market as term loans which are also indexed.
Therefore, it can be seen that reducing the inflation part of investment incomes makes it possible to have a system whereby interest rates on loans are reduced from 0 to 6 per cent, depending on which income tax bracket the borrower is in. It can also be seen that the lower the income tax bracket, the more advantageous the measure is, particularly if your are unable to deduct interests from your income, which is the case for a home owner. Home owners just like small-business men, farmers, fishermen, would see a major reduction in their interest rates, which would be inversely proportional to their income tax bracket. At the current level of inflation, the tax on
The Budget
the inflation component of investment income may be from 3 to 6 per cent, depending on the tax bracket the lender is in, as 1 have just indicated.
That amount would be eliminated from funds invested in indexed term deposits. This reduction would benefit investors as well as borrowers. This system also has the advantage of reducing uncertainties on the real cost of financing, since it will remain fixed over the life of the contract, whatever the inflation rate.
I would like also, Mr. Speaker, to refer briefly to the second proposal in that consultation paper on inflation and taxation of Personal Income, which deals with a registered shareholder investment plan. Canadians could contribute funds to a registered shareholder investment plan with an investment dealer or a financial institution. These funds could then be used to purchase common shares of Canadian corporation taxable shares listed on a Canadian stock market. The sums contributed to the plan would be neither deductible in computing income tax purposes nor taxable when withdrawn. The moneys contributed to the plan would be defined as being the cost of the aggregate of shares held in a registered shareholder investment plan. At the end of each year, the amount contributed would be multiplied by the rate of inflation over the year or since the date of contribution to the plan. The shares would be valued at the end of the year and the inflation adjusted value would be determine the taxable amount. By applying the technique I explained earlier for term deposits, we would have on shareholder investments a real yield that would be higher than the current one. 1 see, Mr. Speaker, that you are getting impatient and I do not want to abuse the time of the House. I appreciate your patience and honourable members' kindness.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to this amendment calling for the resignation of the government at a time of economic crisis in this country, a crisis which, judging by the tone of its debate, the government does not seem to recognize. I listened to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) talk about an illusion, talk about rates of return, talk about savings plans and budget measures and I find he does not seem to have any understanding-in fact, he does not even have the courtesy to give me attention on this matter-that many sectors of our economy are going bankrupt. A financial fire storm is sweeping the country, consuming our jobs, our energies, our savings and our businesses. Yet the government refuses to recognize the seriousness of the situation. It refuses to act. It refuses to move in a positive and realistic way to lay any basis for positive economic recovery.
The problem is very simple. It has not been addressed by this government. The country is simply running out of cash. Our capital is being dangerously eroded. The reason is very clear. The cause of this critical situation, which is forcing the collapse of companies and the loss of jobs, is the failure of the Liberal government to deal with the problems of high interest rates by abandoning the anti-investment tax measures of the last three budgets, and also the Liberal government's failure to introduce tax policies that are firmly and forcefully redirected toward incentive-based savings programs.
The minister has outlined tonight one tentative step in that direction which is a series of tax proposals in the new budget. They have been circulated for study in the investment community. Further study of incentives for investment is like consulting a man whose house is burning to see if he would like a pail of water. The clearest evidence of this economic catastrophe- and for the people affected, it is a catastrophe-are the revised statistics showing the impact of high interest payments on cash flow, the lifeblood of the Canadian economy.
In the first quarter of 1982, all companies in Canada, large and small, paid on average 45.4 per cent of their cash flow on interest costs. One year ago these companies devoted only a quarter of their cash flow to these costs. The impact of interest costs on cash flow has doubled in a year. Smaller companies are hardest hit. This year they are paying on average about half of their cash flow on interest charges, compared to only one-third last year. That is on average, which meant that an awful lot of companies paid up to 100 per cent of their cash flow on interest rates. If you look at the ratio of the percentage of interest rates to entire pre-tax earnings for larger companies it rose to 83.3 per cent in the first quarter of this year. That means companies simply do not have the money to keep going. That is why William Mulholland, chairman of the Bank of Montreal, before the committee hearings on bank profits said the following:
The rolling impact of high interest rates on business must spell more bankruptcies and worse unemployment to come unless some action is taken.
That is why Cal Knudson, Chairman of MacMillan Bloedel, the largest forest company in Canada warns of:
Widespread bankruptcies, a weakening of our financial base and a major collapse that will imperil the financial structure of our country.
That is if the government persists with its policies.
Further evidence of this crisis that we face is the rate of bankruptcies. They are up 40 per cent over last year. The liabilities associated with those bankruptcies are up 100 per cent. Many major corporations, and I include Chrysler Canada, International Harvester, Dome Petroleum, MacMillan Bloedel, Inco and Falconbridge, are barely hanging on. At the same time some of the banks are dangerously overextended in executing some of this government's highly unrealistic policies. The government is going to be called upon to guarantee more loans like that of Dome Canada. Yet it refuses to recognize the peril facing the country.
One critical symptom of the crumbling economy is the emergence of hidden bankruptcies. These are a relatively new phenomenon which is surfacing in the B.C. business community. It serves to hide the fact that thousands of British Columbians are going to lose their jobs because their employers are secretly bankrupt.
During this recession these companies have not been declared legally bankrupt. They have been placed in a status called "soft receivership". No statistics are kept and the firms are never identified. Their status is often known to senior management and often unknown to their employees.
In British Columbia firms in soft receivership include real estate companies, forest companies, property developers and retail companies. When a company faces bankruptcy and has
July 6, 1982

no hope of operating profitably the banks instal a licensed trustee. In the case of soft receiverships, he is often called a management consultant or something which hides the purpose of his duties. He effectively takes control of the business. The management is retained to maintain the appearance that nothing is wrong and to sell off the assets in an orderly fashion. The aim of soft receivership is to avoid selling assets at fire sale prices, and thus secrecy is essential.
The incentive for the banks is to recover their loans. The incentive for business is to keep operating for as long as possible in the hope that enough money may be recovered from the sale of assets to pay off the debt load and to continue the company in a different form. But the fact remains that these companies are bankrupt, that these employees are losing their jobs, and that in the coming months these companies will be quietly, silently and secretly liquidated.
The reasons for this crisis, as I discussed earlier, are the high interest rates which have led to the cash crunch that I have already described. Another major reason is the government's spending which is at a post-war high of 25.3 per cent of GNP. This government has not lived up to the promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to restrain spending to no more than the growth of the economy.
As a matter of fact, if the government had followed that criteria, it would have to reduce its spending this year to match the drop in GNP. This government's policies have also led to the enormous deficit. It is now $19.6 billion instead of $11 billion which was forecast in November. It has led to the situation where one tax dollar in four goes to service the public debt. This has resulted in financial cash requirements this year in the market of $17.5 billion, which has led to the danger of crowding out in capital markets as government borrowing this year will exceed 50 per cent of net new securities placed in Canada. This pressure on the market will keep interest rates high and may send them even higher.
At the same time the government is stripping the savings of Canadians through its tax policies. One leading economist for Pitfield MacKay Ross has pointed out that corporate profits are actually exaggerated by inflation. They are actually at a post-war low, and the effective corporate tax rate is 75 per cent. In some companies, such as those in the forest industry, it exceeds 100 per cent. This profit squeeze is prolonging the recession. The result is the Canadian economy is dangerously under-capitalized because of a lack of adequate common equity and because of capital outflows which have followed this government's policy.
Because my time is limited, I want to refer to what this kind of policy is doing for British Columbia, and in this connection refer to letters I have received from some of my constituents about the impact of these policies on B.C. I have a letter here from an owner of a dance shop on West Broadway. This is a small shop serving the cultural industry. He writes, referring to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), as follows:
He is leading not only business but individuals into bankruptcy. He is sucking not only those of us who work for ourlselves dry, but is gobbling up the savings of
The Budget-Miss Carney
many working people. People who lose their homes through job loss or high interest rates lose their savings and their pride.
I have another letter from a person in my riding who wrote to the Minister of Finance and sent a copy to me. This person writes:
Dear Mr. MacEachen:
This week I got the bad news from the bank that they are not going to lend me any more money and that they would force the sale of my house to pay off a loan. With market and interest rates where they are, the price 1 will get will completely wipe out everything 1 have managed to save since 1 graduated 15 years ago from university.
That is the kind of impact we are receiving as a result of this government's economic policies.
I have another letter here from a woman in my riding who writes:
Young couples today simply cannot afford to have children ... I have been married for ten years. For ten years my husband and I have struggled to get into a position where we can afford to raise a family. Yet the economic reality is that each year the situation gets worse.
She closes her letter to me by asking, "What is happening to our country?" I can tell her what is happening to British Columbia. Its two biggest industries, forestry and mining, are having the worse summmer since the depression of the 1930s. Already some 19,000 IWA workers are out of work, with more to come. Pulp and paper mills are closing and reducing their capacity. The interior forest industry, which is already running at 70 per cent of capacity, is anticipating dropping to 30 per cent or 40 per cent this summer. Peter Bentley, the head of Canadian Forest Products, says:
I see nothing positive for the second half of this year, nor the first half of 1983, even if interest rates were to go down because of the time lag before it gets to us. Prices might be marginally better but to me a turnaround means when you stop bleeding and start operating with positive cash flow.
Most companies in British Columbia are certainly not in that position. At the same time, its second industry, mining, is closing down. This summer there will be an estimated 10,000 workers affected by mines closing down on a temporary or permanent basis. At Cominco in Trail and in Kimberley, 6,300 workers have been affected. Craigmont in Merritt is closing down. Amax, the molymine, has closed down, throwing 432 people out of work. Noranda at Babine Lake is shut for a year. This copper producer will be shut from July 1982 to July 28, 1983. All along Highway 16, all through the interior of British Columbia and on the upper coast, mines which have been major employers have been shut down.
We know that the problem is not entirely domestically created, that it is partly due to falling metal markets and the lack of housing demand in the United States. These industries were looking to the budget as the last hope for some help, particularly with their cash flow. There has been no help for mines. IWA indicates that the housing assistance program will be of "minimal benefit" to employment in British Columbia. As a matter of fact, the housing program will barely take the production of one of our major mills.

July 6, 1982
The Budget
Recently in Prince George I visited a machine shop of a metal fabricator who employed 220 workers last year. This year he has laid off everyone except his core people. This man has been in business for 20 years. He has had no orders for two months, no orders at all. Of course this means that he has not been able to order steel from eastern Canadian mills. I told him that if he obtained an order he was to call us. I asked him to call us because he was our leading indicator, and if we knew that he was obtaining orders, we would know that the economy was starting to be revived. That was two weeks ago and we have not received a telephone call. He still has not obtained any orders. This man cannot believe what is happening to him. He did everything right. He spent 20 years of his life and 20 years of his energies, and he is going down the tubes. That kind of situation is developing all over B.C.
What was the Liberal response in the current budget to this kind of economic tragedy? It was mostly the same measures as last time, with a few changes. The measures were the same as those in the catastrophic budget which created many problems for the Canadian economy. This budget keeps the half-year rule for capital cost allowance, which is a measure that seriously affects many, many companies. It retains the taxation of employee benefits and northern allowances, which in British Columbia amount to $3 per hour in extra tax. No wonder we in British Columbia cannot be competitive when we have to bear that amount of extra tax load. There has been no resurrection of the MURB program. As a matter of fact, the budget measures are forcing the cancellation of many MURBs and the actual bulldozing over the MURB sites, with a loss of housing stocks and investor savings. Some measures were postponed, such as the insurance measure and the restricted interest expense which my colleague outlined. Many measures were referred to this new committee for study before implementation. The result is more uncertainty, more confusion and more delay.	.
There is still no leadership, no help for the economy and no direction. There has been merely a reaffirmation of damaging Liberal policies and the spreading by Liberals of false assumptions and misinformation. One false assumption is that Canadians will practise restraint when government spending soars. How can they? Another piece of misinformation and false assumption is that a recovery will occur in the third or fourth quarter.
